The primary method used to tabulate election vote totals relies on manual counting of ballot tallies, which are scanned images of text containing vote quantities.  The process involves human readers using optical character recognition (OCR) techniques to convert the images into usable numerical data for accurate calculation of election results.  A crucial yet underdeveloped aspect of this process is the validation of obtained data, which is essential for the integrity of election outcomes.  To address this need, a new approach called informed OCR (iOCR) has been developed to integrate detection tools with traditional OCR software to enhance its performance and accuracy.  A case study involving the tabulation of ballot tallies from a gubernatorial election in a small town in the United States was used to test the effectiveness of this method.  The results showed that traditional OCR methods failed to produce reliable data due to its limited accuracy, which was significantly improved with the implementation of iOCR, which also offered additional benefits of increased speed and reduced costs compared to traditional methods.

In deep learning models with time series data and linear architectures, a unique phenomenon called "benign overfitting" can occur. Our research discovers that over-parameterization plays a key role in leading to these sparse solutions. When a linear model is trained on past data with a limited number of features, the process of minimizing loss becomes remarkably efficient, bypassing the requirement for regularization to control model complexity. This is the key insight our research seeks to explore. We demonstrate that even with unlimited data, models can still exhibit benign overfitting, meaning that without over-parameterization, they would fail to generalize. Additionally, we show that specific components, such as batch normalization and residual learning, contribute to increased flexibility in the model. To address this, we propose a linear normalization layer that integrates aspects of batch normalization within a time series framework, resulting in more controlled model behavior. Our research on benign overfitting aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion on generalization in deep learning models and provide a comprehensive analysis of a previously unexplored use case.

The attention bidirectional long short-term memory (BLSTM) model is a relatively recent technique used in single-channel speech enhancement models. In this work, a complete attention bidirectional deep learning structure that integrates a range of advanced signal processing techniques and machine learning models is proposed and its effectiveness is demonstrated through comprehensive testing using the DITSL dataset. The proposed structure is characterized by its complex architecture that incorporates multiple layers of bidirectional attention mechanisms allowing for the implicit extraction of speech spectral features. Furthermore, a comparison with the original BLSTM model revealed that our proposed structure achieves a notable improvement in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) values and is particularly adept at handling noisy speech samples with SNR levels as low as -6.0 dB.

A recent discovery of a deadly fungus infecting bats through bioacoustics highlights a previously unexplored threat where microorganisms spread diseases using bioacoustic mimicry of social sounds, potentially targeting a wide range of animals via this method. We investigate the breadth of this threat by analyzing bioacoustic properties of bioacoustic signals produced by microorganisms and compare them to animal social sounds across various species and environments. Our research reveals that the fungus, batrachochytridium dendrobatidis, stands out for its unique sound characteristics that closely match the frequency range of bat calls, in contrast to other fungi with different sound frequencies. This finding suggests that B. dendrobatidis' acoustical properties are specially adapted to target bats, and may indicate that other microorganisms could be exploiting bioacoustic channels to infect other animals and plants.

A key factor in modeling decentralized energy markets is the ability of storage technology to enable flexible and effective management of varying energy supply and demand. By leveraging storage, operators can balance supply and demand across different time periods. We build on previous research by Koptu and Bieckus, model storage technology as a tool for managing risk through self-allocation across different time periods. Our analysis focuses on a two-period model with uncertain demand and separate storage technologies for each period. We utilize a robust approach, incorporating storage technology as a means of mitigating risks associated with demand uncertainty. Our analysis provides an in-depth examination of how storage technology impacts social welfare and identifies key drivers of this impact. Furthermore, we investigate the implications of storage technology on market outcomes and find that it leads to increased investment in other technologies, offsetting any negative effects on welfare due to reduced risk aversion.

In quantum systems, electron wave packets that arise from core excitations can provide crucial insights into electron behavior. This study utilizes x-ray pulses from the SLS and highly sensitive electron yield measurements to investigate the time-dependent intensity of an Auger electron spike. A newly developed theoretical model, taking into account electron interactions and the characteristics of an electron orbit, effectively explains the experimental findings. It reveals that electron yields can reveal the intricate structure of an electron wave packet and may prove useful in investigating other quantum phenomena associated with core excitations.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and shapes of the planet. To better understand these experiments, multiple factors are varied in the model, including the temperature difference between the equator and the poles, the strength of solar energy, and the properties of atmospheric gases. Despite these influences, the primary findings show that atmospheric circulation patterns are largely determined by two factors: the rate at which the atmosphere rotates and the temperature differences between different latitudes. These discoveries shed new light on research about atmospheric circulation in smaller planets and offer a framework for examining the effects of varying conditions on atmospheric circulation in these environments.

Large convolutional neural networks have achieved exceptional performance in the ImageNet classification benchmark. However, addressing a related problem - few-shot image classification - has proven challenging. Despite the close relationship between these problems, existing approaches typically treat them as separate entities and rarely leverage insights from one area to inform progress in the other. In this work, we address both issues simultaneously by exploring dynamic learning strategies in the ImageNet context. Our investigation reveals that several such approaches accelerate convergence in large-scale ImageNet training. Notably, one strategy, using a start-up learning period with a smaller batch size, proves equivalent to multiple-shot image classification. Our findings encompass new contributions as well as a thorough examination of existing methods on both FewShotImageNet and ImageNet classification.

A fundamental concept in linear algebra and control theory, the RHP is extensively explored in the context of transfer function stability properties. A pivotal tool in analyzing these properties is the algebraic and geometric multiplicity of a system's pole. This study introduces novel relationships between the algebraic and geometric multiplicity of a pole and the index of the system's minimal realization. These connections are expressed through the determinant of specific matrices and reveal important insights into the underlying geometry. Consequently, this research establishes new constraints on the algebraic and geometric multiplicity of a stable system, particularly one with a right-half plane pole.

We propose an unconventional method of using dipolar condensates in a one-way quantum computer to efficiently measure phase using a combination of beam-splitter interactions between two separate condensates. To achieve this efficiently, we must effectively create paired bosonic states through a process of interacting with a cavity filled with a small number of photons. To this end, we develop a technique of generating paired states using a series of applications of the beam-splitter interaction, starting from an initial state where the condensates are unconnected. We show that this technique leads to an increase in the paired state amplitude as a function of the number of applications, going from an initial state where the condensates are unconnected. We also demonstrate that this technique can be applied to create states with high levels of squeezing. Notably, we find that our proposed method surpasses the optimal pair-production efficiency achieved through conventional beam-splitter interactions between two connected condensates, especially in scenarios involving few photons.

Donors offer a beneficial combination of long coherence time, small error rates and decent control over operations. However, isolated phosphorus donors have inconsistent and slow operational characteristics when trying to build a multi-qubit system based on donor exchange. It would be beneficial to account for interactions between donors, to reutilize exchange effects that could otherwise decrease the error rate. We then created a simplified method that can efficiently model multiple donors, based on a variable-convergence approach that utilizes the results of exact simulations. Our investigation focused on the conductance of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by the Dirac-Weyl theory. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) constrictions in the sample were examined using Raman spectroscopy and tunneling measurements. When the electrical field is low, the conductance through both large and small-sized constrictions follows Ohm's law, indicating a robust, gapless energy spectrum. However, when the electrical field is high, an anomalous, non-Ohmic behavior is observed, which varies depending on the sample and only occurs in small-sized constrictions. The conductance in these areas can significantly exceed the expected value based on the local potential variation. This discrepancy may be related to transport phenomena in mesoscopic channels or require a different theoretical explanation.

Wireless communication systems can make significant contributions to preventing road accidents through alert message transmission, particularly in high-risk areas like road intersections. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has shown promise for 5G systems, and our proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol enhances VC's message delivery performance in this application. In a scenario where vehicles on intersecting roads generate interference, our analysis assesses the reliability of alert message transmission under ACN in a setting without and then with interference. Notably, ACN outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives like ICN and CoNOMA-Aff in terms of lower bound eliability function values at road intersections. Numerical simulations confirm our theoretical findings, indicating that ACN provides a more dependable solution for preventing road accidents through alert message transmission.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink transmissions based on real-time traffic patterns, enabling more flexible and efficient TDD configurations.  We propose a new method for scheduling called Game-Theoretic Model Scheduling (GTMS), where an evolutionary algorithm determines the optimal TDD parameter settings to maximize throughput and minimize delay.  Our results show that GTMS leads to significant improvements in average throughput and reduced delay in comparison to traditional fixed TDD approaches.  Moreover, GTMS exhibits robust performance in response to varying initial conditions and topological changes within the cellular network.

Despite numerous theories, there has not been a clear understanding of the Hall anomaly observed in type-II superconductors. Our research analyzes the magnetic field's effect on the Hall anomaly in a YBCCO thin film using a different measurement technique, and we find the measured values to be significantly higher than previous recordings. We found the vortex-vortex interaction to greatly influence this phenomenon. In a highly dense vortex state, the speed at which vortices move is comparable to the lattice site distance, indicating the need to consider point defects within the lattice. We propose a new model accounting for the impact of these defects on the vortex lattice dynamics. This model includes an increased viscosity effect and a new force resulting from the defects, and we found it capable of explaining the observed data from both the thinnest films and more densely packed samples.

Using the exact field theory for the Ising model in the presence of an external magnetic field, we find that various moment-based observables in the three-dimensional Ising phase transition exhibit a fixed point as the critical temperature is approached from either the cold or the warm side. By analyzing susceptibility and higher-order moment coefficients, we gain insight into how standard universality properties are realized. Our calculations also enable us to evaluate moment cumulants at criticality, showing that while central moments behave similarly to the standard Ising model, the moment-to-moment relationships do not. Furthermore, by integrating the field theory with the method of stochastic boundary conditions, we confirm that the fixed point is a feature of the critical surface itself.

A characterization is provided for a specific type of commuting square that generates a finite-index, finite-depth subfactor, specifically one with a non-trivial and simple structure. Additionally, a particular type of prime factor, represented by the von Neumann algebra $R_\infty$, is characterized in terms of its central operator system and a particular property.

In this work, we introduce a novel neural network framework based on Hamiltonian dynamics, which we call Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs). Our HNN model utilizes a unique neural structure where the input is processed through two separate but interconnected neural layers. We then derive an expression for the input's partial derivative, which can be computed solely from the network's output and intermediate layer. This distinct property enables our model to effectively learn input derivative computations in conjunction with function predictions. We demonstrate HNN's efficacy by successfully replicating the purpose and performance of multiple benchmark experiments that previous research had already successfully achieved using other methods. Furthermore, our HNN model is capable of processing sensitive data without needing to accommodate input restrictions and significantly outperforms existing approaches in speed and parameter efficiency for specific tasks.

In complex decision-making systems with numerous stakeholders, the issue of trust becomes crucial when artificial intelligence models make pivotal decisions on behalf of others. The problem is particularly pronounced in situations like autonomous healthcare delivery systems. Research has been done on developing algorithms that cooperate with artificial intelligence through the negotiation process, the activation of human agents in artificial intelligence networks, and the creation of scoring systems to evaluate the performance of artificial intelligence models accurately. However, more research is needed on a critical aspect - building artificial intelligence models that are trustworthy in the first place. A collaborative approach between artificial intelligence agents is proposed to address this challenge. The system features a cluster of learning models that collaborate, where each agent represents a subset of similar data cases. A method called federated learning was implemented to train the models collectively using each agent's individual dataset. When the system makes decisions, each agent assesses the outcome's reliability. If the outcome is deemed unreliable, the associated model is updated through the addition of new data case. This approach is demonstrated with a healthcare delivery example. The proposed system addresses the challenge of constructing artificial intelligence models that are trustworthy in complex decision-making systems involving multiple stakeholders.

In x-ray based prohibited items detection, achieving high accuracy in real-world scenarios is difficult due to varying image quality, different angles, and a wide range of item categories. This research addresses these challenges by introducing a novel lateral inhibition module to enhance model performance and a high-quality benchmark called HighFou (HFou) for prohibited items detection. The module's design is an adaptation of off-center feature extraction, incorporating a unique lateral inhibition path to focus the model's attention on central objects within the image. It's integrated into a detection framework known as the Lateral Inhibition Feature Aggregation Network (LIFAN), which outperforms existing models on the MSMT-Prohibited-Benchmark and HFou benchmarks. LIFAN's performance indicates that its detection results improvement is specifically attributed to improved performance on medium to large sized items within the image. The research also discovers that current models struggle with detecting low-quality and rotating items, along with highly transparent or metallic objects that don't show up clearly on x-ray images, or items that are poorly positioned within the image frame.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is presented for links in a thickened torus. This polynomial displays the same properties as the original colored Jones polynomial, including being unique and umbral, with a dedicated extension for knots. Furthermore, research indicates that a specific modification of this polynomial, when evaluated at a root of unity corresponding to a high-dimensional volume, provides estimates of a link's volume that align with computer simulations and known volume formulas for particular shapes. The novel nature of this polynomial is demonstrated by deriving a specific instance, the 2-colored version, through a known construction method, whereas the general formula for this polynomial remains unknown.

Context-gloss enhancement is a novel approach to address the word sense disambiguation challenge.  We leverage contextual language models to enhance the glosses of polysemous words in a sentence, thereby facilitating their proper identification.  Our approach's core innovation lies in the use of masked language models to post-pend the context to existing definitions found in word embedding resources, thereby augmenting them for more accurate sentence classification.  We employ BERT and SPBERT as context-gloss enhancement models, and through exhaustive experiments on the SemCor dataset, our approach is shown to outperform the baseline models including the current state-of-the-art method by a significant margin of 3.5%.

The reciprocal Gamma function is analyzed and a genuine integral representation is derived for its values excluding those on the negative real axis. Moreover, an examination is conducted of the associated division theorem for negative integers and specific fractional cases.

This letter details the LHC's ability to detect top quark production in proton-lead collisions, considering a range of proton-proton collision energies from 5 to 13 TeV and lead-nucleus energies from 1.36 to 10 TeV, corresponding to nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energies between 5 and 13 TeV. Top quark production can be identified by observing the sequence of decays from the top quark to a bottom quark and electrons or muons. To accomplish this, this study establishes minimum bias selection criteria, defines strategies for top quark reconstruction, and evaluates relevant proton-proton reference data, including top quark production rates. Lead-proton collisions are compared to proton-proton collisions at the same energy levels to determine the signal-to-background ratio for top quark production. Furthermore, this letter provides the cross-section calculation formula for top quark production in proton-proton collisions, incorporating a transverse mass threshold, in addition to the acceptance and efficiency correction factors required for top quark reconstruction.

This study focuses on key variations in text-to-SQL syntax and seeks to
integrate auxiliary tasks to enhance semantic understanding across domains.
Initially, a basic text-to-SQL model is established using BART, and its
limitations are identified when applying it to a different domain. To tackle
this issue, specific tasks are incorporated to provide support and aid in
the interpretation of semantic structures. These tasks encompass null value
inference, column name identification, and condition table identification,
along with the primary task of constructing SQL code. To facilitate learning
across domains, a shared latent variable is introduced through an auxiliary
round-trip task, connecting the text-to-SQL model to a database management
system. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on the Pseudo PASCAL dataset,
a PASCAL dataset with additional null values, and the actual PASCAL dataset
to demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach over baseline models.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy in networks, focusing on educational and research applications, and highlights the challenges and limitations of DP in this context. It is necessary to protect sensitive information within networked data, which can be achieved through DP by limiting the revelation of details about individual data points. However, applying DP in networks proves complicated due to the need to balance privacy protection and preservation of meaningful statistical information about the network structure. Several studies have explored the integration of DP and machine learning in networks, revealing that incorporating node-specific information in private learning can compromise the accuracy of results. Therefore, research has shifted towards leveraging network structure in a way that does not depend on node-specific data, which is where the field of graph-based learning comes in. This trend is reflected in the increasing interest in semi-supervised learning on graphs, which uses private training data to inform predictions on target nodes. Another area of research within network differential privacy is joint private analysis of networks, which allows multiple privacy budgets to be combined, even if private algorithms have not shared information about each other. This paper also explores various other challenges facing network differential privacy, including difficulties related to data diversity, interoperability, and interoperability, as well as several potential avenues for further research.

The vast amount of data that Euclid will generate in order to achieve its objectives, constitutes a significant resource for the development of cutting-edge expert services. In accordance with traditional principles of transparency and data reuse, Euclid is fully committed to disseminating its comprehensive data sets to various third-party platforms. Within the framework of this approach, various heritage science applications will have the opportunity to benefit greatly from accessing Euclid's satellite imagery featuring high spectral resolution of the sky. Euclid's operational infrastructure is set to provide invaluable resources for conducting sophisticated analyses of its image databases using high-performance computing platforms. Furthermore, Euclid's community-driven approach, supported by extensive software development kits and documentation, will facilitate seamless customization of its software tools. In the field of heritage science, Euclid is poised to make groundbreaking contributions, particularly in the areas of cultural asset management, heritage site monitoring, and urban planning.

In this research, a method is designed to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous last-mile delivery technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a challenging network as one with specific characteristics, such as tightly curved sections, parallel roads, and intersecting roads with sharp turns. To ensure randomness, we develop a statistical approach to measure the complexity of a road design and a sampling algorithm to produce a variety of challenging networks. Our results demonstrate that roads generated through this system mimic those created by human experts and offer a diverse range of complexity levels. This system has the potential to enhance testing of autonomous delivery systems in simulation by producing high-quality, challenging road networks.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. Existing approaches to recommending music focus on sequence-based models, which struggle to incorporate additional descriptive information. Our research introduces the concept of music captioning, where descriptive narratives are generated to complement personalized playlists. In this study, we develop a novel music captioning model that leverages both audio content and metadata to produce engaging descriptions. Our model's performance is evaluated on a newly created dataset, yielding promising results that showcase its potential to enhance the listening experience through more effective recommendations.

Building on quantum hydrodynamics, our approach represents a random fluid dynamics that accounts for both the uncertainty principle and quantum interactions within a Bose gas. By incorporating the hydrodynamics method, we derived a set of linearized Navier-Stokes equations that reflect both the random nature of quantum fluctuations and the interacting particles' effects. Our research extends the conventional quantum hydrodynamics methodology, first proposed by Damadori et al., to account for the randomness seen in actual quantum fluctuations. We demonstrated that our approach leads to a more accurate representation of superfluid properties and demonstrated its applicability by investigating a specific random quantum hydrodynamics scenario. Our framework offers a chance to explore other random conditions of quantum hydrodynamics.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address these issues, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for refining proposals through context aggregation at the proposal level. Our work has been thoroughly evaluated using the ActivityNet v1.3 dataset, achieving State-of-the-Art (SOT) results on benchmark versions ActivityNet V1.3 Val and ENet V1.3 Val, and nearly SOT performance on the more demanding ActivityNet V1.3 Test.

This work investigates the generation of palm tree modes in the JET tokamak.  A specific ELM type, referred to as a "type-I" ELM, can cause the onset of these chaotic magnetic phenomena when intense edge currents localize to specific locations.  Similar edge conditions exist in the KSTAR tokamak, which also exhibits type-I ELMs and corresponding edge localizations.  Notably, eddy currents induced by a private beta-related mechanism, which are present in both tokamaks, share comparable magnitudes to those generated by the localized currents that give rise to type-I ELMs.  Therefore, it is proposed that the private beta-related mechanism contributes significantly to the origin of these currents, increasing the risk of palm tree mode formation during future operating regimes characterized by low edge currents and high plasma pressures.  A code simulation demonstration illustrates this potential risk in the upcoming JET ITER-like W device.

This research focuses on collision avoidance for mobile robots working together in a shared environment. A novel approach has been proposed that combines dynamic vortex potential fields with sensor data to create a collaborative collision avoidance system. By leveraging the unique paths generated by the proposed method, it becomes possible to create a field that can be shared among the robots, facilitating communication and mutual understanding to prevent collisions through collective action. Both theoretical and practical aspects of this method have been tested with positive results.

Consider a long sequence of letters generated from a source text, assuming that the text complies with a given language standard. Our research focuses on analyzing frequency patterns found in subsets of averaged letter combinations within extended sequences. Ultimately, we establish two main large deviation principles to describe the long-term behavior of averaged frequency measures of dependence within these combinations, taking into account the inherent correlations present. Our findings address previous studies raised by Denoeuf and by Bouchon and by Bouchon and Daudin.

Recent advancements in intelligent reflecting surfaces have the potential to significantly improve the performance of radar systems. By actively reflecting radio waves, these surfaces can interact with the target in a controlled manner. This study focuses on wave-based target parameter estimation in the presence of an intelligent reflecting surface. To achieve this understanding, a mathematical model is established and existing methods are applied to analyze and optimize the performance of intelligent reflecting surfaces. Our research utilizes the maximum eigenvalue method and eigenvalue distribution characteristics to determine optimal reflector configuration. Furthermore, numerical results and simulations demonstrate the capability of intelligent reflecting surfaces to enhance target parameter estimation.

Comparative assessments of fuzzers are uncommon due to the inherently unpredictable nature of mutation-based testing, which can be influenced by factors such as test case length, performance, and coverage. Our research aims to address this gap by formulating a systematic approach to evaluating and distinguishing between different fuzzing techniques based on their behavior with respect to specific program properties, which we call "fuzzing traits". We utilize this framework to appraise and differentiate among various state-of-art fuzzers in terms of their characteristics, which are demonstrated through practical evaluations using a suite of benchmark programs and various testing metrics. Our findings reveal varying traits across different fuzzers, which are further validated by our empirical results showing how certain attributes correlate with testing outcomes. To facilitate replication and further research, our evaluation data, including intermediate execution data and coverage metrics, are freely accessible for download.

Pretrained neural networks have been successfully applied to few-shot learning tasks in continuation with minimal loss of performance. Notably, a study used the MiniMiniImageNet benchmark, which was introduced earlier, consisting of 80 classes from the MiniImageNet dataset, leaving out 80 other classes for the test phase. The evaluation assessed the model's ability to learn new classes without a significant decrease in performance on previously learned classes. Interestingly, when attempting to add new classes to the existing ones, the results showed that the accuracy on previously learned classes significantly dropped below 50%. This drop in performance raises concerns that the method is not truly learning new classes as expected. A further investigation was conducted which discovered that, when using a fixed backbone network, the performance on previously learned classes actually decreased when trying to learn new classes. This counterintuitive finding suggests that a more challenging baseline is needed to validate the effectiveness of the method in learning new classes.

We establish a fundamental result that enables us to determine whether a given surface, minimizing the area within a specific homotopy class in a metric space, is unique up to a certain type of transformation. This achievement is made possible by adapting a previously proven uniqueness criterion to suit surfaces in metric spaces. Additionally, we expand the scope of our result to include surfaces with boundaries by applying techniques of surface compression and re-embedding.

This final installment concludes our study of one-dimensional heat equations with discontinuous initial conditions, specifically where the boundary values at positive and negative infinity are distinct. Building upon earlier findings, we examine solutions with initial data that converge to distinct limits. If the equilibrium solution is unstable, we find that solutions far from the equilibrium will eventually behave like the one closer to zero, with time-dependent oscillations. This result expands our understanding of solutions with convergent initial data, covering cases where the equilibrium is stable, neutral, or unstable.

Recent studies on 64Ni have revealed new insights into the phenomenon of shape coexistence in stable nuclei. Excited states of this nickel isotope, which exist in a spherical or prolate shape, have been examined using a global interaction model with a monopole force. This analysis at zero spin has allowed researchers to understand the driving forces behind coexistence in these low-lying states. By testing different single-particle energies, calculations have demonstrated that shape coexistence in 64Ni is primarily fueled by the monopole force. However, a complication arises due to the influence of the zero-spin pairing, which needs further disentanglement.

Approximately six years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced Lipshitz games, a class of games whose payoffs rely on a player's distance from a specific reference point. The parameter controlling this dependence is the Lipshitz constant, effectively limiting how rapidly a player's payoff can change. In their work, they demonstrated that combinatorial games featuring bounded Lipshitz constants possess combinatorial equilibria, provided a particular condition is met. However, the article at hand investigates whether this equilibrium can be identified through a combinatorial method, specifically by querying a specific component of the game. Our findings indicate that the answer is negative, as we demonstrate the existence of instances requiring an exponentially large number of queries to locate an equilibrium of this type. The approach used to achieve this result also enables us to generalize previous research on Lipshitz games and yield new insights regarding the relationship between a game's connectivity and its ability to support approximate fixed points.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, predicted values are greatly affected by variance, making the process ineffective. Our experiments demonstrate that using a larger J-k fold cross-validation method can significantly reduce variance issues. We advocate for the use of a non-standard leave-one-out version, effectively eliminating variance concerns. Our findings suggest that adopting this approach yields more reliable results and facilitates effective feature engineering.

Recently, machine learning models have achieved great success in various tasks by leveraging knowledge from pre-trained models through few-shot learning. Despite the benefits, significant challenges remain in leveraging large amounts of instructional data, a common issue across multiple formats including text, images, and speech. This trend has given rise to innovative architectures that enable learning from instructional data, often described as "instructor-student" models, where the student learns from the instructor's guidance. The field of computer vision has led the way in adopting this architecture, followed closely by natural language processing. This study aims to explore the vision models that employ instructor-student architectures, examine their applications, and discuss their theoretical foundations within the context of computer vision.

We introduce a new efficient approach for solving exact MPE in graphical models by utilizing a unique representation of functions. Our proposed method can also be applied to address constrained MPE efficiently. By utilizing this new framework, we derive specific algorithms to solve MPE exactly in two hours for MPE instances that couldn't be solved by current state-of-the-art methods in a week. Our approach can also find optimal solutions to NP-hard problems that were previously unsolvable. We demonstrate that our representation of functions facilitates the reformulation of MPE as a set of linear inequalities under equality/inequality constraints, enabling us to employ highly efficient linear programming solvers to find exact MPE solutions and optimal solutions to NP-hard problems quickly.

The investigation of light-matter interactions at the atomic level is crucial for a wide range of applications, including quantum communication and metrology. By examining the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam, we gathered evidence of photon recoil and its associated kick back to the light source. This phenomenon significantly impacts the measurement of key physical properties, such as the mass of a particle and the speed of light, which need to be accounted for in future precision measurements using cold gases.

When shear stress exceeds a certain threshold in a suspension of solid particles, synergetic thickening occurs, leading to rapid increases in viscosity. This phenomenon, common in geological and industrial applications, is characterized by a first-order phase transition from a low-viscosity fluid to a highly viscous one. Research on a dense, hard sphere suspension has revealed that frictional forces alone cannot explain the shear thickening transition, and that particle collisions play a crucial role in amplifying the effect. A novel mechanism has been identified, where the collisional energy is converted into additional friction, leading to a self-perpetuating feedback loop that drives the transition. A theoretical model has been developed to capture this new mechanism, and successfully predicts the global scaling of the shear thickening transition over a wide range of shear rates and densities. This model demonstrates that the transition should be independent of changes in density for a specific scaling of shear rate, and that this scaling can be achieved by adjusting the shear rate based on the density. Experimental data confirms that the shear thickening transition exhibits scaling when considered in this new light.

The Racah algebra can be viewed as a central extension of the semi-direct product of two copy of $A_1(1)$ Yangians, $Y(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, with their 5-dimensional representation. By examining the central extension, we find a relationship between the central elements of the Yangians and the Fock space. Furthermore, understanding this relationship enables us to determine the irreducible representations of the central extension by categorizing the central elements of the Yangians. Additionally, we are able to identify a specific set of central elements for the symmetric square of the fundamental representation of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, and we note that this result is a specific instance of a more general phenomenon.

Our study shows that in a bilayer hexagonal magnetic material, low-lying triplon
excitations can lead to twisted-phase supersolid and superfluid states. This
happens due to the interaction between triplons and adjacent layers, which causes
the spin waves to couple and form a complex, symmetry-restricted Hamiltonian.
To understand this phenomenon, we develop an umbrella-vortex theory, which
reveals that the twisted-phase supersolid and superfluid states can be achieved
at very low temperatures along with the stabilization of the umbrella-vortex
and twisted-vortex states. The predictions made here can be tested with
experimental techniques such as NMR, ultrasound, and Raman spectroscopy, which
can provide insight into the twisted-phase supersolid and superfluid states,
which are rare phenomena that have not been observed before in experimental
studies.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-recoil experiments, specifically focusing on WIMP-germanium interactions and 1 GeV WIMP energies. We examined how the velocity of incident WIMPs affects the angle of recoil in relation to the direction of their initial path. Utilizing a variety of initial velocity distributions, we found that the distribution of this angle can be controlled by the ratio of the WIMP's reduced mass to that of the target nucleus. We also found that this distribution is generally independent of the specific details of the velocity distribution. Furthermore, we found that the distribution of the recoil energy in relation to the angle of the WIMP's initial path is largely unaffected by the velocity distribution. We found that the most significant constraint on the detection of 1 GeV WIMPs is not the velocity distribution but rather the relatively low efficiency of most detectors for detecting small recoil energies, below 5-6 times the typical electronic recoil threshold.

A crucial aspect of a democratic search engine is the visibility of unbiased information, particularly when searching for politically sensitive topics. This concept is often referred to as "informational diversity of search engines." However, studies have shown that users may not always have access to the most relevant information due to search engine personalization. To quantify the extent of missed information, we designed a series of experiments where proxy users searched for predefined topics using Google's Web search with and without the personalization feature enabled. The results showed that, on average, users failed to find at least 18 out of the top 20 most relevant results when personalization was enabled. This drop in accessibility highlights the need for search engines to strike a balance between providing personalized results and ensuring access to unbiased information.

We are exploring the concept of a cutting-edge particle collider that could revolutionize understanding of fundamental physics beyond the current Higgs regime. By examining potential for new physics in both high-energy realms (high-energy, high-momentum transfers) and rare processes (low-energy, low-momentum transfers), we reveal a comprehensive landscape that incorporates various theories such as supersymmetry, extra dimensions, and certain exotic scenarios. In this report, we delve into specific rare processes, including flavored Higgs boson production, lepton-flavor violating processes (e.g., muon to electron conversion or muon decay), and certain CP-violating processes. We also examine prospects for discovering new physics at a muon collider, particularly useful given that a future SNS or ILC will provide highly accurate measurements of muon properties. Lastly, we outline potential for a muon collider to improve understanding of fundamental physics across a broad spectrum of theories and phenomena.

A novel technique has been introduced to create and evaluate a respiratory motion-corrected 4D T2-weighted MRI sequence, originally based on a classic 2D T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) method. By incorporating a novel signal processing approach called k-space residual correction (kRC), this evaluation aimed to assess kRC's performance in correcting respiratory motion in 4D TSE MRI. For this purpose, a 4D TSE MRI sequence was developed using a breath-held approach in four phases, and kRC was applied to correct motion in each 2D slice. Further modifications enabled free-breathing acquisitions, yielding high-quality 4D TSE MRI images comparable to those obtained through gated imaging. By extending kRC to 4D, this study demonstrated effective correction of respiratory motion in 4D TSE MRI, facilitating the creation of detailed anatomical maps essential for cancer treatment planning.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing secure control systems for complex, dynamically changing processes. It addresses a significant challenge in control systems research, namely ensuring the system's stability when its behavior is unexpectedly altered, often as a result of cyber attacks aiming to destabilize the system. To achieve this, the paper introduces a new concept called Control Barrier Functions with Input Constraints, which provides a clear, quantitative framework for defining the secure operating parameters of a system. It also outlines a straightforward method for applying this concept to systems that can be modeled using polynomial equations. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through the development of a secure control system for a flight simulator. It demonstrates the importance of considering the limitations of a system's input controls when designing its control barriers. It also shows that the proposed approach can successfully prevent the system from entering an unstable state in response to sudden, unexpected changes.

In mathematics, approximation theory uses to generalize various concepts from topology by utilizing a set's natural hierarchy to define fundamental properties. Our work develops a novel approach to defining topological properties based on how regions relate to each other in a gradual, comparative framework. By applying CF-approximation spaces, we create a framework that enables the identification of spaces with specific topological characteristics and establishes connections to existing theories of general topological spaces.

We develop a new testing framework for the association between two datasets, particularly tailored for categorical data, with applications in genome-wide association studies and electronic health records analysis. Our approach leverages paired-permutation testing to assess hypothesis significance, incorporating antithetic variate theory to enhance power and reduce computational costs. Theoretical calculations provide an alternative method for estimating critical values, with proposed adjustments for categorizing data. Our findings demonstrate that the adjusted method surpasses the accuracy of the theoretical calculations, with the benefit of negligible additional computational expense. We showcase the effectiveness of our framework through simulations and a case studies involving genome-wide association studies, in addition to analyzing electronic health records data in search of genetic factors associated with coronary artery disease.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the three primary shipping routes: Europe-Japan, Europe-New York, and Europe-Singapore.  This dataset addresses the existing research limitation in the shipping industry, which hinders the development of sophisticated theories and models.  A set of key variables' descriptive statistics and correlations are examined to ensure they are generally consistent with the principles of neoclassical theory.  Asset pricing models are tested and found to produce inferior results, while the CCAPM model shows improvement, and the CCAPM model with an endogenous gamma produces the best results.  A further analysis of the data using the Ljung-Box test reveals the existence of a strong seasonal effect in the freight rate returns, and the subsequent arima-garch model produces more reliable results.  A further examination of the data using the arima-garch model reveals the existence of a strong seasonal effect in the shipping quantity and used ship price returns.  A CCAPM model with an exogenous gamma model produces the best results for the freight rate returns, and an arima-garch model produces the best results for the shipping quantity and used ship price returns.  A further examination of the data using the arima-garch model reveals the existence of a unidirectional Granger causality from shipping quantities to freight rates and used ship prices, and

Given any surface that is being traversed by a closed curve, we can define the "loom area" as the minimal area that the surface's projection onto a plane must occupy, assuming the projection is made by mapping the surface's points to their closest equivalents on a nearby plane. Lomania allows us to prove that a specific type of surface triangulation, known as a veering triangulation, will always have a specific area when it is derived from a specific type of surface and boundary data. This connection is particularly notable when the boundary data consists of two intertwined curves. By extending previous research on loom areas, our research demosntrates that a particular combination of surface, boundary data, and triangulation can minimize or maximize the loom area when compared to other similar combinations. This result is proven to have a connection to number theory, providing insights into the behavior of numbers generated by the surface's area calculations.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. One critical performance booster is model parallelization, which involves subtaining a central model and a decentralized counterpart for each node. However, this approach is limited by significant message passing and increased computational demands. In an effort to overcome these challenges, a technique called learned sparsification was developed. This method involves training a reduced model that maintains connectivity with only a limited number of neighboring nodes, achieving substantial reductions in computation and memory usage. One notable example of this technique was Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) which is commonly used for semi-supervised node classification. For instance, on the Cora dataset, using 16 nodes proved 1.3 times more efficient in terms of computation and 1.5 times more efficient in terms of memory than the centralized model, while also yielding 97% of its accuracy.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where further information about the input vectors is acquired after the sketches have been constructed, as it is vulnerable to an attack that manipulates the sketches by as little as $\sqrt{n}$ times without being detected, a problem exacerbated by the fact that many algorithms involving sketches assume the ability to detect the largest entries with a margin of $n$. Interestingly, we have discovered that reducing the attack's impact to $n^{1/4}$ time the original vector is achievable, proving it is $n^{1/4}$-hard to accomplish, and proposing an efficient $n^{1/2}$-approximate solution to this problem. Our findings are complemented by an equivalent issue involving finding the maximum length of a non-zero vector (modulo a specific equivalence), a problem that, interestingly, can be settled for counts sketches but remains unresolved for standard sparse recovery techniques.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be removed through a process involving a combination of Riemannian surgery and a topological adjustment, effectively allowing for the extension of Donaldson's work on positive scalar curvature to closed manifolds containing compact singular spaces. In this continuation of that research, we expand the scope to consider manifolds with boundary, demonstrating the possibility of removing compact singular spaces from a Riemannian manifold with positive scalar curvature.

A critical reevaluation of the Nernst effect in vortex liquids is presented, based on a combination of theoretical model and experimental data. A key finding indicates that the anomalous Nernst effect in vortex liquids can be fully understood by taking into account the influence of magnetic field on the vortex dynamics and lattice structure. Two distinct mechanisms contribute to the anomalous Nernst effect: the first one is related to the interaction between superconducting vortices and normal spin currents, resulting in a normal spin Hall response; the second one originates from the interaction between superconducting vortices and the normal spin viscosity, giving rise to a spin viscosity response. It should be noted that this type of response also occurs in chiral superconductors. Additionally, the work shows that the normal spin Hall response and spin viscosity response are closely linked, demonstrating that the sum of the two responses is consistent with the entropy conservation principle. Furthermore, our findings imply that the superconducting vortex lattice exhibits a non-trivial, mobile entropy that cannot be captured by a conventional Ginzburg-Landau approach.

Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time control. This paper proposes a proactive framework for predictive control, enabling swift decision-making by aggregators in response to changes in the grid. A key component of this framework involves modeling the release of real-time flexibility through an online estimator that provides immediate feedback to the controller, facilitating rapid adjustment of energy usage. With minimal knowledge required from the operator, our framework leverages learning algorithms to optimize flexibility deployment across repeated instances, with results validated through simulations of adaptive load management in real-time.

The recent interest in stock value prediction can be attributed to the potential for financial gains and the scarcity of time-series data in financial modeling. A recent development in natural language processing known as BERT has proven highly effective in analyzing less structured data. In this research, we combine BERT with generative adversarial networks to develop a novel approach to stock value prediction. Initially, text data containing historical stock value information and trading volume is converted into input features. Next, a BERT-based classifier accurately forecasts future stock values within a short-term period. To achieve this, we modified a BERT-based classification model to anticipate stock values above or below predetermined thresholds. Furthermore, a generative adversarial network was integrated to enhance model performance. Our results demonstrate that this hybrid model outperforms traditional methods in stock value prediction tasks.

Recently, a groundbreaking new method was introduced, transforming both traditional $e$-folding envelope formalism and the new scattering approach into equivalent concepts.
This study builds upon this discovery and expands the scattering approach to accommodate multiple phenomena, including both relativistic and non-relativistic jet configurations, as well as radiative and conservative stages of energy transfer.
By integrating the new method with existing models, we leverage their established characteristics to derive key parameters and apply them to various scenarios of jet dynamics.

Our research analyzed the production of double Higgs boson resonance in future electron-positron colliders, specifically exploring their capability to discern new physics signals associated with the Higgs boson within the context of Effective Field Theories. By focusing on the Standard Model itself and its most popular beyond-Standard-Model theories, we investigated how TeV-scale $e^+e^-$ colliders could reveal new physics interactions in the Higgs sector. Our study revealed that these colliders excel at investigating Higgs couplings to fermions, offering interactions with a sensitivity of around $0.25$ to $0.30$ times the Standard Model value, depending on the specific context. Concerning Higgs self-interactions, we found that these colliders could provide a sensitivity of approximately $0.15$ to $0.20$ times the Standard Model value. Moreover, we found that $e^+e^-$ vs. $pp$ colliders have distinct advantages, notably in the production of double Higgs boson resonance and triple Higgs production, as well as in investigating Higgs couplings to light quarks.

When general relativity is coupled with matter fields, forming the Einstein field equations, certain modifications lead to theories of metric gravity. These amendments can be made metric-affine by introducing a torsion tensor, which arises from the presence of spinny matter. This paper explores two types of modifications to the Einstein-Hilbert action: firstly, modifying the Einstein-Hilbert action to include a torsion term results in the Einstein-Cartan theory; secondly, modifying the action to include a quadratic term leads to a new theory of gravity. Both of these modified actions are palatable when coupled with non-spinning matter.

A new computational framework is introduced to speed up the calculation of localized shocks in a five-dimensional space that mimics anti-gravity. By simplifying a complex set of equations, researchers can quickly determine key properties of these shocks. It's shown that when two separate shocks meet, the time it takes for the interaction to become stable can be predicted using a basic set of rules. Additionally, the properties of the resulting shock can be broken down into a series of predictable components.

We investigated the anisotropic drag experienced by a cylindrical object moving through a granular medium, specifically a fluid-saturated granular bed, at varying speeds and distances from the bed's surface. Our research shows that the anisotropic drag becomes less noticeable as the cylinder's speed increases, and its magnitude decreases with greater distance from the bed's surface. Our findings indicate that the anisotropic component of drag can be influenced by the bed's surface curvature and the presence of a fluid, although the exact impact needs further exploration. Notably, the curve of drag vs. speed exhibits more pronounced irregularities when measured from the side than from above.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation drives gas outflows in its central regions. Our data show a large-scale outflow with a distinctive "bipolar" shape, affecting a vast 25-kiloparsec area. We took a novel approach, focusing on a 1-kiloparsec "core" region around the galaxy's center, to investigate how star formation rates are influenced by outflows in this area. Our findings revealed that regions with high star formation rates were located along the outflow's "head," suggesting that energy released by star formation may contribute to the outflow's creation. This relationship may not be unique to this galaxy, as it is a key aspect of a well-known theory about how star formation and outflows interact. We also discovered a crucial connection between outflows and the formation of molecular gas rings that are sites of high-star-formation-rate regions. This relationship may be a critical factor in explaining how outflows regulate star formation in galaxy centers.

Current evaluations of machine learning models rely heavily on accuracy metrics such as AUC-ROC and Brier score. Yet, complex systems like healthcare recommendation platforms often have numerous, inaccessible data points due to their large number of participants. Additionally, such systems typically involve multiple variables that significantly impact the model's performance. As a result, evaluating models for such applications often requires evaluating the model's performance on a large number of data points, making it expensive in terms of time and human labor. To address this challenge, we present BoGraph, an innovative approach that uses limited training data to establish a graphical model of the system's behavior. BoGraph achieves this by leveraging human expert feedback on the data points they have access to. When faced with new, unseen data points, BoGraph uses Bayesian optimization to determine the system's most likely behavior and make predictions accordingly. Our approach has several key advantages over conventional evaluation methods. Firstly, it can handle complex systems with many variables and data points due to its low-dimensional Bayesian framework. Our research involves collaborations with healthcare companies that use recommendation platforms. For instance, in one such collaboration, BoGraph evaluated the effectiveness of models for recommending effective treatments to large cohorts of patients based on various medical conditions. Our results show that BoGraph outperforms conventional evaluation methods by a margin of up to 5 times in terms of efficiency. Our approach is efficient enough to support iterative model development processes, enabling teams of researchers to test and refine models in a data-driven, collaborative process.

Our research examined the triangular flow's behavior within a given event plane in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions using a multiphase transport model. Initial observations indicated that the triangular flow's magnitude increases with an event by factor ratio $\xi_n$, which shows a stronger dependence on centralality in smaller Cu+Cu collisions. Furthermore, when analyzing the triangular flow's component aligned with the elliptical event plane, our findings revealed that it exhibits negative valence and growing magnitude with $\xi_n$, as well as increased centrality, which suggests an underlying symmetry in heavy-ion collisions.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more comprehensive and diverse datasets being continuously added to the web.  While this content is rich in information for machine-based applications, evaluating the data quality remains an unresolved issue.  To tackle this problem, a comprehensive approach has been developed that assesses the quality of RDF datasets based on three key factors: data reliability, data reliability, and application performance.  A suite of advanced tools has been created to facilitate the evaluation process and ensure scalability.  Our results demonstrate that our approach yields superior quality improvements, with datasets benefiting from up to 300% quality enhancement.  Our research offers a pioneering contribution to addressing data quality issues in the Linked Data era.

When working with stochastic processes observed at fixed time intervals, a fundamental challenge arises in estimating parameters when data is missing. This issue becomes particularly significant in applications where system observations are limited or missing due to sensor failures, system saturation, or digital recordings. A common approach in statistical analysis involves likelihood-based estimation methods, but they are not feasible for processing discrete data without first interpolating the stochastic process to a continuous timeline. This limitation leads to a significant increase in computational costs. In contrast, our proposed approach skips interpolation, instead applying a discrete data likelihood function directly. By leveraging specialized numerical algorithms, this approach enables the estimation of parameters at a much lower computational cost. We evaluate this method using simulated data and real-world examples, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency. Notably, our results indicate that discrete estimation methods can yield more precise outcomes than their continuous counterparts.

We analyzed spectral data for 38 Seyfert galaxies to reexamine the relationship between gas ionization and the direction of their central black holes. A key finding is that in many cases, gas is being ionized from a direction perpendicular to the line connecting the galaxy's center to a nearby emission region. This discovery challenges current models of gas ionization in galaxy environments. It suggests that gas ionization is influenced by external factors such as gas flows and the presence of star formation, rather than being solely determined by the direction to the black hole's accretion disk.

As mobile devices and IoT equipment grow in number, edge computing is emerging as a middle ground between data generation and remote cloud storage.  This shift creates opportunities for real-time analytics closer to data sources. For example, monitoring temperature changes, traffic patterns, and sports events become feasible with edge computing. However, processing data in real-time at the edge relies heavily on evaluating events instantly. If event evaluation is delayed, the entire edge application is impacted. Current approaches to event evaluation, based on traditional transaction processing techniques, often lead to decreased performance and limited scalability. In response, we introduce a new approach, called Continuous Evaluation, to speed up event evaluation. Continuous Evaluation leverages in-memory technology and pipelined processing to process events quickly. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Continuous Evaluation through a monitoring use case and evaluate its performance against a distributed database system. Our results show that Continuous Evaluation achieves significant improvements in throughput and reduced processing times.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider LHC has been actively searching for signs of CP violation and rare decays in beauty meson events since 2015, combing through data from 2015 to 2018 for relevant candidates. By examining a specific rare decay of $B_s$ mesons where a photon and a muon are emitted, ATLAS researchers found a statistical discrepancy that warrants further investigation, with the observed occurrence rate being 3.3 standard deviations away from predictions. Additionally, searches for another rare $B$ meson decay, characterized by the emission of a muon and an electron, yielded results consistent with theoretical expectations. As for CP violation in the charm meson system, which was previously found to be absent, ATLAS data reconfirms this finding with heightened precision.

The generation of realistic traffic scenes through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual objects into predefined scenes, but this 
does not account for the diverse range of actual environments. In contrast, our 
proposed system, SceneGen, crafts entirely new scenes from scratch by utilizing 
road network blueprints and extensive datasets of real road features. SceneGen 
leverages a unique set of tools, including a special kind of neural network 
called a graph neural network, that allow it to generate authentic scenes by 
imitating the training data. When put to the test on a large, complex dataset 
called BDD-TRAIN, SceneGen demonstrated a level of quality and variety that 
outpaced even experienced human designers.

On a Cayley tree, we modify the Ising model's interaction potential to an exponential form, $V(x,y)=\epsilon$ when the distance between sites $x$ and $y$ is one. We demonstrate that this modification leads to a periodic state on the Cayley tree with finite height, and this periodic state reduces to a biperiodic state when the tree's height is infinite. Furthermore, we prove that these periodic states minimise energy among all possible states with specific lattice symmetries.

A critical aspect in preserving numerical invariants of a differential equation is time-stepping scheme choice. Although high order methods may be desirable for accuracy, stability and monotonicity preservation can be achieved with lower order methods that maintain essential structure. A major limitation of these methods is the restriction to equal time step sizes for different equation components. A new approach has been developed that allows for flexible time stepping, enabling the use of more accurate methods for specific parts of the system while maintaining preservation of the original structure. A case study with the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation demonstrates that this method can lead to a significant increase in computational efficiency compared to traditional methods.

A combinatorial approach to establishing combined ergodicity for sequences of operators has been established, extending a significant result by Dai, Li, and Yang, who utilized this approach to achieve combined ergodicity for a specific class of sequences. Our work expands upon their findings, broadening the applicable conditions and ultimately leading to a key conclusion that a specific criterion, previously shown to guarantee mixed ergodicity, is also sufficient for combined ergodicity to occur.

We simulate the evolution of a single N-type molecular cloud in a dwarf galaxy throughout a 10 million year timespan, modeling the growth of dust grains within the molecular cloud and its associated HII region.  By accounting for the effects of external radiation on dust grain growth and evolution, we observe a three to four times increase in dust mass compared to models ignoring this factor.  The resulting simulations reveal significant disparities in dust grain size distributions between the molecular cloud's core and its outer regions.  The presence of these disparities is supported by observations of far-infrared spectra in low-metallicity galaxies.  Our simulations also predict the formation of supernovae that create dense SNII environments, further facilitating dust grain growth through stochastic processes, leading to additional increases in dust mass.  The predicted maxima of 1000 $M_{\odot}$ for dust mass and 10$^{10}$ cm$^{2}$ for dust continuum emission in these systems have implications for the broader field of dust grain evolution research.

Detecting and classifying objects in images has achieved remarkable accuracy over the past decade, with the use of deep convolutional networks particularly effective. However, a key limitation of existing work in this area has gone largely unaddressed - the majority of research has focused on identifying objects within a relatively short distance from the camera, with little consideration given to situations where objects are farther away. In reality, people frequently find themselves in far-field scenarios, with for example drivers often traveling at high speeds with little awareness of upcoming road signs. Current technology falls short of helping these individuals, with potential dangers arising if it does not improve. In an effort to address this gap, researchers introduce a new task called Far-Field 3D Object Detection (FF3D) and present a cutting-edge approach called Far3Det, with the goal of making their work more practical for real-world use cases. Far3Det demonstrates superior performance to existing detection methods when tested on multiple datasets, with the achievement of particularly impressive results on the PASCAL 3D+ dataset - with the inclusion of far-field annotations for training and evaluation. With Far3Det, the team has also explored the benefits of novel loss functions tailored to FF3D, with the hope that their work will pave the way for safe and reliable 3D object detection in far-field scenarios.

In this study, a quantum machine learning approach was applied to develop a chemical state predictor, which can generate highly accurate ground state wavefunctions for molecules and solids using limited numerical data. In tests with commonly studied materials, the model achieved exceptional results, producing highly precise total energy values and lattice parameters with little to no training, and efficient state reconstruction from limited Monte Carlo samples. It also demonstrated the ability to predict excited state properties through transfer learning with only a few training samples for certain materials. The study shows that quantum machine learning can effectively reduce the computational burden required to study complex systems on quantum computers.

Soft-tissue ultrasound imaging finds use in various clinical applications, such as reconstructing soft-tissue abnormalities found on imaging, pre-surgical planning, and guiding interventional procedures.  Accurate image registration is essential for these procedures, but it is complicated by the soft nature of tissues, which can lead to poor results due to image degradation, tissue deformation, and low ultrasound frequency.  We have developed a novel approach to align ultrasound images of soft tissues with pre-operative surgical surfaces, specifically for partial nephrectas.  Our approach uses a biomechanical model that takes account of fluid dynamics to describe the movement of fluids within tissues, but we have also created a unique shortcut model that quickly processes high-definition images in real-time.  This shortcut model is trained on vast datasets of nephrectas images and surfaces, and has been successfully tested on a significant group of patients, showing that it can align ultrasound images with a high degree of accuracy and speed.

For a stationary, spherically symmetric spacetime, research has focused on conformal matter collineations within the energy-momentum tensor. The overall structure of these collineations is determined under non-degenerate conditions, with fifteen distinct, independent conformal collineations found. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the associated conformal collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Moreover, specific degenerate cases can yield infinite degrees of freedom in non-degenerate scenarios, highlighting the critical nature of non-degeneracy within the energy-momentum tensor.

In this work, we tackle the problem of estimating scene flow by addressing a critical issue in current methods. Relying heavily on pretrained features that are often chosen for their classification capabilities can lead to inaccurate flow predictions due to the inherently different nature of the task. To overcome this limitation, we propose a unique Self-Supervised learning framework that forges alternative feature representations tailored to the scene flow task through a process of adversarial learning. This approach allows our model to extract flow-related features from the dataset in a spontaneous manner. We pretrain our model on the EuRoC dataset and achieves state-of-the-art results on the KITTI2012 and KITTI2015 test sets without fine-tuning or additional training. Notably, our results outperform SSFlow, the current leading self-supervised scene flow estimator, on all subcategories of the KITTI2012 and SOTA self-supervised and masked-encoder methods on the KITTI2015.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, using the MIT bag model and considering the magnetic field's influence on quark masses. We derived the thermodynamic potential of spin-polarized strange quark matter and subsequently analyzed its free energy under a finite temperature and strong magnetic field. By minimizing the free energy, we obtained the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter. Our findings indicate that density gradients along the magnetic field direction can occur in spin-polarized strange quark matter. Building on the work of Farhi and Jaffe, we examined the stability of spin-polarized strange quark stars and found that static, spherically symmetric stars can be described by equations that include the influence of temperature and quark mass changes due to the magnetic field. We discovered that quark stars can be stabilized in an unstable environment if their baryon number exceeds approximately 178.6 barB GeV^-1, and that temperature and quark mass changes can lower the stability barB by about 10.6%, given a specific quark mass configuration.

A subset of cubic graphs that is uniquely identifiable through the property that every 2-factor can be configured to align with a specific arrangement, will be referred to as type B4 graphs in this context. It has been determined that all type B4 graphs can be colourized using a minimum of 3 different edge colours. Additionally, it has been found that a Hamiltonian cycle exists within every type B4 graph, and every type B4 graph that contains an ideal 3-edge colouring will be named as G3.4. The term ideal 3-edge colouring can be defined by the criterion that every 2-factor of the graph is composed of three distinct colour components. It has been established that G3.4 graphs and bicubic planar graphs that contain an ideal 3-edge colouring, exhibit isomorphic characteristics.

We examine arrangements of linear subspaces within a higher-dimensional space, specifically focusing on those defined by collections of hyperspaces in the form ax + by + cz = 0 in three-dimensional space.
