Our analysis also considers non-trivial solutions to this equation and its variations, including forms where the coefficients are subject to additional constraints. Leveraging our understanding of these arrangements, we explore the idea that a specific type of polynomial, when evaluated using integers as inputs, will yield prime results. One key scenario we explore is the case where the polynomial is expressed as the sum of two simpler polynomials, one of which has a specific form that can be factored easily. Another scenario we explore is the case where the polynomial is a product of two similar polynomials. Building on previous work by Hartshorne, our findings provide evidence towards a broader conjecture that any arrangement generating a specific type of vector, known as a torsion point, within a particular space will consist of components that are part of another specific type of vector, known as a non-torsion point.

This paper introduces a novel approach called Timeloops to efficiently train an automated system call filtering module for containerized applications. Timeloops is designed to effectively learn a policy for system call filtering within a limited time frame, doing so by exploring relevant call data from a comprehensive set available in the past. To achieve this, we've developed a data-driven method called Windowed Mutual Information (WMI) to concentrate on calls with the most significance to policy goals. Furthermore, we've integrated WMI into an iterative learning framework called LoopOpt, enabling optimized call data utilization and a reduction in training time. Our experiments showcase that Timeloops outperforms a leading machine learning method in both efficiency and performance. Additionally, we've implemented Timeloops in a tool called OptCall, a flexible and adaptable solution that has been put into practice by a leading open-source service platform. OptCall has successfully been put into use and has been submitted for review to the Kubernetes community.

Investing global $B-L$ symmetry with three gauge bosons, which includes a dark gauge boson, significantly impacts the dark sector. A simple, yet thorough, exploration of this augmented Standard Model reveals that the most compelling dark matter model is a pseudo-Goldstone boson, mediated by the dark gauge boson within a coset of $SU(2) \times SU(2)$. This paper delves into the details of this model, which includes the distribution of the dark matter mass, the distribution of the distribution of the dark matter mass density, and the production of the pseudo-Goldstone boson through both the dark gauge boson and the W boson. Furthermore, this model is in line with the requirements set by the Relic Abundance, Direct Detection, and Higgs Decay constraints.

In this study, a modified random finite state space model (RFSSM) was developed to improve the probability mass function (PMF) estimator. By segmenting the origin space into defined areas, the RFSSM grid-based model (GBM) estimator provides a more precise prediction of target location than conventional methods. We analyzed the GBBMs' scalability and flexibility, discussing various configuration options and implicit implications. Furthermore, integrating the GBBM with a Gaussian-based birth model (BMBM) estimator resulted in a comprehensive target tracking framework capable of managing sensors in an optimized grid-based structure. Simulations validated the GBBM's scaling benefits and effectively utilized available computational resources, thereby improving overall system performance.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior decay term. By first transforming the model into a new form involving the adjoint system, and then establishing key estimates using the Carleman estimate technique, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame.

Utilizing player positions from previous game moments enables effective ball control, and our proposed approach achieves remarkable results in life-threatening situations on the field by effectively guiding players in ball possession techniques. By successfully securing possession of the ball in $57.03\%$ of life-threatening situations and generating $34.51$ meters of distance from opposing players over an average of $5.56$ seconds, our model demonstrates notable improvement over conventional control systems.

In seismic imaging, estimating source and medium properties from seismic data is an enhanced method that complements traditional reverse time migration. This approach has the advantage of naturally incorporating nonlinearity in both source and medium, but it's a highly complex problem to solve. Researchers have typically applied linearized versions of this method for improved accuracy, but such versions fail to capture the medium's extended source effects. This work proposes linearizing the source function while keeping the medium's properties fixed, essentially treating the source as extended within a single frequency cycle. This approach has the benefit of enhancing imaging results without the significant computational expense associated with full linearization, but it does require the accurate estimation of initial conditions. If successful, this method could provide high-quality seismic images using realistic source models. This project is ongoing, with future plans to discuss scaling issues, modify the synthesis method, and conduct more extensive numerical tests.

In the context of quantum optics, we examine how an interplay of linear loss and beam splitter interactions influences the polarization of light. We find that combining these operations results in the creation of quantum squeezing in orthogonal modes of symmetric cavities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon of quantum squeezing can generate optical asymmetry. We develop a full characterization of the quantum squeezing and optical asymmetry by factorizing the covariance matrix of the system. Specifically, we identify the conditions under which maximum quantum squeezing and optical asymmetry arise. Our research provides a framework for studying quantum effects in biological systems, inspired by the work of H. M. Vasu and C. N. R. Rao.

We have presented the results from AstroSat data during the Type-I outburst of the low-mass X-ray binary system IGR J19294+1816 in October 2019. Timelines were created from the data of the flat-field detectors in the three spectroscopic instruments - ABUBY (ABU is the abbreviation for three Indian instruments Abubler, Abucollar, and Abuzaid that include ABS, BU and Aburqai'a, respectively) and cyclotron line features were analyzed using the Abrupt Transition Model in HEASO Rydoft. Features at ~11.2 keV and a QPO frequency of ~0.036 Hz were discovered. This the first QPO of its kind discovered in this binary system, a type known as a mHz QPO.

In demographic models with noise, the interaction between competing species can lead to exclusive occupancy or coexistence in multi-species environments. Our research supplements existing findings by examining a competing species that colonizes more effectively than it competes. When the competing species is present, the first species faces increased local extinction risks and heightened colonization benefits. This leads to a tradeoff between competition and colonization. When the noise is low, the first species is driven out by a higher risk of local extinction. However, in noisy conditions, the first species exploits its colonization advantages to dominate. Moreover, when all species have equal colonization advantages but differ in their competition costs, a specific subset of species can coexist in noisy environments, as they occupy different niches defined by their competition costs.

Ancient cultures utilized sundials for timekeeping, and their legacy continues in modern times through remaining historical artifacts. Although many sundials have disappeared, some still exist in various settings like museums, historic sites, and private locations across Indonesia. This project aims to document and study Indonesian sundials with a mobile app called Suryakala-Nusantara, which collects and calculates local time using sundials located at various latitudes across the country. The app can account for any errors in sundial construction and provide accurate time based on the true solar time. It also includes a map feature showing how sundial time differs from standard time in Indonesia. The app has already recorded over 200 sundials, and users are encouraged to contribute their own locations and contribute to the study of Indonesian sundials.

A Reflecting Surface-Aided Integrated Data and Energy Networking (RIS-AIDEN) model is introduced to optimize an objective function that combines data transfer efficiency and energy harvesting efficiency. Within this model, an evolutionary algorithm is proposed to manage a cognition system consisting of multiple agents, each representing a node in the network. These agents share similar goals, centered around maximizing their respective individual objective functions by making critical decisions regarding whether to engage in cognition activities, exchange data with neighboring nodes, and utilize energy harvested from their environment. Furthermore, a novel decentralized approach is designed to facilitate learning for these agents within the RIS-AIDEN framework, an area that previous research has largely overlooked. To evaluate the performance of this system, numerical simulations are conducted under both non-cognitive and cognitive scenarios, revealing improved outcomes for the latter. Additionally, an analysis is provided to illustrate the convergence of the proposed learning algorithm.

This research investigates the possibility of using a single-point LDV system located away from the area of interest to acquire two-dimensional measurements. By positioning the probe far from the desired area, the technique aims to take advantage of the short coherence length of LDV to filter out only the local flow field. However, the challenge lies in determining the optimal timing for data collection. To tackle this issue, this study proposes a novel approach based on the flow velocity fluctuations in the proximity of the probe. The proposed method involves setting the start and end points for data collection in relation to the local flow velocity in the proximity of the probe. To test this approach, the study uses data from previous experiments conducted by other researchers, featuring LDV measurements in a turbulent jet flow. By applying the proposed method, the study demonstrates its effectiveness in accurately determining two-dimensional velocity profiles using a distant LDV system. Compared to measurements taken with a co-located LDV system, the results show a maximum error of 6.3%, whereas without the proposed method, the error would be as high as 46.4%.

The introduction of programmable electronic phase plates (PEPPs) marks an important advancement in transmission electron microscopy (TEM), enabling controlled modulation of electron phase in annular dark-field imaging. By doing so, it significantly enhances atomic-scale mapping of material structures, particularly for materials lacking a clear contrast-down-to-the-atom level. To further optimize PEPPs, researchers propose an approach that involves training neural network-based models in simulated electron microscopy data, leveraging computational electron optics. When tested against previously developed static phase plates, the trained models demonstrated improved performance in correcting spherical aberrations and distortions, as well as enhancing contrast and mapping accuracy. Notably, this method allows for the creation of custom electron phase masks that can correct for both spherical and coma aberrations through optimization techniques. Furthermore, applications of this method are explored for time-resolved imaging and cryo-TEM.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. Our experiments involve training and evaluating state-of-the-art transformer-based dialogue models on the Optimal Role Assignment Reading Comprehension task, introducing novel metrics centered on role-based prediction, and testing the impact of pre-training these models with optimal response targets. Our findings highlight the critical importance of judging the reasonableness of encoder representations through comprehensive comprehension tests to ensure the robust performance of dialogue models.

LiDAR data analysis in the context of mobile robot navigation is focusing on local destination place recognition. This task requires creating a 3D descriptor that can distinguish between repeated areas along a navigation route. To achieve this, a novel deep learning-based LiDAR place recognition system is proposed, incorporating an innovative range-wise attention mechanism. The model's performance was tested and compared to established methods using the KITTI dataset, resulting in improved accuracy and efficient processing.

Video transcode is a critical function in the distribution industry, serving as a prerequisite for the playback of encrypted video content. To investigate the potential benefits of moving transcode processing to the cloud, this research involves comparing cloud-based processing against traditional, on-premise encryption methods using a testbed based on standardized components. The study also develops an empirical model to predict the performance of cloud-based transcode, considering factors like processing power and network latency.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic screening in doped graphene sheets over a wide temperature range, from absolute zero to high temperatures. This finding is critical for assessing the thermal screening effect in graphene devices, especially when combined with a new heat capacity formula derived from the Bose distribution. Our theoretical model demonstrates that the heat capacity of doped graphene can be determined through a single material parameter, the Fermi temperature, which characterizes the thermal screening effect. Numerical simulations demonstrate how the thermal screening modifies the spectral density of the electron density of states in comparison to its zero-temperature and high-temperature limits. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the thermal screening effect significantly influences the spectral density at intermediate temperatures.

Intelligent virtual agents, able to converse freely with humans in a natural and fluid manner, are still a subject of ongoing research in both speech generation and dialogue systems. While significant breakthroughs have been achieved in isolated tasks like single sentence speech synthesis or single turn human-conversation mimicry, there is still a notable gap between current technology and human-like interactions. To bridge this gap, this work proposes a novel speech dataset called MaskedSpeech, centered around human-read audiobooks with selectively obscured text passages. Audiobooks serve as an ideal testing ground due to their unique characteristics: they comprise lengthy continuous human speech produced in a controlled setting of quiet environments, free from background noise, and feature a diverse cast of human readers. The dataset's design includes a unique masking strategy, where each word is replaced with a random character, varying in case (upper case, title case, or lower case), to effectively capture the disparities between spoken and written languages. Evaluations of an open-source speech synthesis system, leveraging MaskedSpeech and a supplementary dataset called LJSpeech, reveal that incorporating MaskedSpeech leads to a notable improvement in speech quality, particularly in terms of naturalness and overall performance.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes an anharmonic oscillator. We also examine the symmetry of the underlying equation and use it to identify and characterize modes that are stable or neutrally stable.

Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories that incorporate multiple symmetries in a more sophisticated analysis, similar to the approach taken with solitons in gauge theories. In this paper, we explore this complexity by investigating a dual Gaillard-Bern theory, which features two spontaneously broken symmetries within a scalar doublet. We validate the consistency of the model using both unitary gauge and 'c-core' Q-ball theories and proceed with a detailed analysis of core structures. Our findings indicate that core energies can be minimized when energies from both symmetries are considered, potentially leading to further reductions in energy through more complex configurations, such as 'double c-core' structures.

In a cyclic cosmology, matter domination must eventually give way to a phase of dark energy-driven expansion. However, due to the universe's cyclical nature, a cosmological constant-based model is not sufficient to produce the required acceleration. We present a dark energy model based on an unusual property of cyclic cosmologies, where a complex relationship between the Hubble rate and the universe's age allows us to create a model that avoids the need for a cosmological constant. Our model involves a nonlinear boundary condition that defines the Hubble rate as a function of the universe's age, effectively behaving as a dark energy component that drives the universe towards a phase of acceleration-driven expansion in its later cycles. Furthermore, we show that this model can be achieved by modifying the gravitational potential in a specific way, effectively treating dark matter as if it has a 'holographic' property. We demonstrate that this model meets the observational standards for dark energy models, fitting various observational data sets comfortably. It also predicts specific signatures, such as a nonlinear relationship between the Hubble rate and the universe's age, that could be tested using existing and future astronomical observations.

Gnutzmann and Smilansky previously developed a formula for calculating the bond scattering matrix of a graph using a method that involves a complex Hermitian matrix. In this work, we modify their approach to accommodate real symmetric matrices, thereby deriving a novel algorithm for determining the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of such matrices. In the process, we also derive a formula to calculate the Dirichlet eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors for a specific type of Hermitian matrix. Additionally, we apply this method to a specific class of matrices that are not in normal form and derive a formula for their spectral resolution. Furthermore, we explore connections between the matrix approach and traditional methods of calculating the scattering matrix and Dirichlet eigenvalues of a graph.

We derive new conclusions regarding the nature of non-commutative, finite Galois extensions of Q that are linked to number fields with a specific property - having a specific cyclotomic algebraic closure and only roots of unity as its Galois group. Our findings expand on famous theorems proved by Leopoldt, Diaz, and others. Additionally, we provide novel evidence supporting the unimodality of certain sequences associated with these non-commutative fields, a concept initially observed by the third author in a previous study. Our conclusions also include bounds on the norms of specific elements within these non-commutative fields, a topic initially explored by the second author in a prior work. Our approach to these results relies on a combination of computational techniques and theoretical proof.

A semi-analytic and numerical technique is used to analyze hadronic uncertainties in ALP (Axion-Like Particle) searches from $B$ meson decays into invisible or dislocated final states. Our research focuses specifically on the Belle II experiment and involves a detailed analysis of $B \to K^n$ decays to compare dislocated and invisible ALP signals. By incorporating the effects of the ALP and applying the $K$-$N$ distortion, we calculated the relevant form factors and spectral functions. We found that the standard $K$-$N$ distortion is insufficient to distinguish ALP signals in $B \to K^n$ decays from the typical $K$ background. To differentiate these signals, we need more precise data or additional information about the ALP spectrum.

This study investigates the utilization of contextualized language models in detecting
altered semantic meanings in paraphrased sentence pairs. Our analysis reveals that
these models are not effective in this task when trained on a dataset with
established evaluation metrics, specifically achieving below-par performance on all
metrics when compared to a simple learning-based approach. However, our research
also sheds light on potential issues with the semantic preservation evaluation
framework used in previous studies. Furthermore, we present two novel evaluation
frameworks grounded in contextualized language models, including one that leverages
semantic role labeling. Our work discloses a notable challenge in the field,
namely the current absence of high-quality training data tailored to semantic
preservation in paraphrased sentence pairs.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) offer an opportunity to study the unique properties of ultralight bosons through their interaction with photons in the vicinity of massive black holes.  By examining a sample of 739 quasars with high spin rates, we gather statistical evidence to support the existence of ultralight bosons with a mass in the range typical of axion dark matter (DM).  Assuming that a significant proportion of these extreme spin systems are a result of solar-mass ultralight boson condensates, we find that the distribution of ultralight DM spin states is consistent with an randomly oriented field.  The proportion of ultralight DM configurations that exhibit extreme spin states, as seen in these quasars, is found to be around 0.01-0.1%, a range that is in line with the predictions made using the photodisintegration model of cosmic ray acceleration.  The predicted frequencies of ultralight DM in the range typical of axion DM (around 10^-21 eV) is found to be between 0.01 and 0.1 times the standard value, a range that is in line with the predictions made using the model of ultralight DM via gravitational wave emission from high-spin black holes.  Our findings provide a strong case for the existence of ultralight DM with a mass in the range typical of axion DM and offer a significant breakthrough in the quest to identify the fundamental constituents of dark

A distinctive feature of neural tissue development is the periodic expansion and contraction of cell nuclei as they move between the upper and lower surfaces of the embryonic brain and retina in zebrafish. Through high-resolution, high-speed imaging, our research reveals that the typical distance traveled by nuclei in one cycle and the time it takes for a complete cycle remain constant in the central zebrafish retina. However, this pattern does not hold true in other areas of the retina or in different brain regions. To gain a deeper understanding of these phenomena, we analyzed the movement of nuclei in the central zebrafish retina and found that their pattern of expansion and contraction cannot be predicted. Instead, their position changes randomly, meaning their path is stochastic. Using mathematical modeling, we found that incorporating randomness into our model accurately explained the nuclei's movement. Our research also shows that imposing a tight surface layer constraint on the nuclei's movement, as well as maintaining a consistent time frame for cell cycle and DNA replication, is crucial.

In this research, we address both color image demosaicing and video reconstruction from incomplete measurements, focusing on codes that facilitate separable image processing. A new code type, called the separable image processing code, enables efficient and stable image recovery through independent component analysis (ICA) from a restricted measurement set. We demonstrate that this code ensures reliable and distortion-minimized image separation, satisfying certain conditions. Specifically, our code guarantees that ICA output contains a single image vector, and this image is both the original data and a transformed version of the original. We show that two established code constructions, based on random subsampling and compressive sensing, meet the required conditions. Notably, our theoretical findings and numerical experiments indicate that separable IPCA codes outperform previous state-of-the-art approaches in both applications.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active liquids with particle-scale inhomogeneities in dimensions greater than two. This model demonstrates how a strong, long-range nematic interaction can overcome the debilitating effects of inhomogeneities in higher dimensions, leading to a divergent nematic correlation length and non-analytic behavior in its dynamic nematic susceptibility. Crucially, this improvement in nematic order does not come at the cost of increased compressibility. Instead, the compressibility remains finite and can be influenced by adjusting the inhomogeneities' strength. Our findings also predict that the nematic susceptibility will display a more pronounced response to inhomogeneities in three-dimensional active liquids than in higher dimensions.

Researchers in academia often team up to produce high-quality research, and their collaborations can have significant impacts, but also present opportunities for malicious activities such as data theft. When academic professionals form new connections, a new temporary network emerges, and understanding the structure of this temporary network can provide valuable insights into potential security risks. Recent studies have focused on static analysis of academic collaboration networks, but they fail to account for critical aspects such as the temporary nature of networks formed during conferences, the importance of conference size, and the impact of network evolution. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to analyzing the temporal aspect of these networks, using mathematical expressions to describe the time-dependent attack and error rates, and verifying our method using data from CCoMiner, a mining conference with a long history. Our research reveals the distributions of node degrees and edge weights, reveals how the attack rate varies over time, and shows that the error rate can be significantly reduced by considering the temporal aspect. Furthermore, our study has policy-making implications, highlighting the need for continuous security awareness campaigns, tailored to the evolution of conference attendance, and prioritizing the security of highly connected nodes.

Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "extraordinary van Hove singularity" (eVHS), 
where an unusual energy maximum occurs on a metal, leading to 
the absorption of electron energy and a reduction in superconductivity. 
We suggest that eVHS singularities are responsible for the 
electronic and magnetic phenomena observed in underdoped cuprates. 
The eVHS model predicts that certain materials can exhibit a critical 
point where they transition from being insulating to superconducting, 
and this model can also explain why certain eVHS singularities 
can only be observed at very low temperatures. 
The eVHS model can also exhibit a type of symmetry known as 
"symmetry protected criticality", and it provides a reason 
why some cuprate materials may prefer to become anti-ferromagnetic. 
The eVHS model can be a useful tool for studying and understanding 
the complex electronic and magnetic properties observed in cuprate 
materials, and it may also be applicable to other types of 
materials that exhibit similar phenomena.

This paper details a specialized device designed for use in physics research, specifically to study spallation neutrons in Aberdeen's underground laboratory. Located in the Aberdeen Tunnel, this laboratory has exceptionally low background noise, situated as it is in Scotland's geologic foundation far from major streets. To investigate spallation neutrons produced by proton beams hitting metal targets, our project employs time-of-flight spectroscopy to analyze the detected neutrons. Neutrons released in the experiment's initial phase are of primary interest as they contain information on the production process. To filter out these early neutrons, our device utilizes a novel approach where the detection system is activated only after a set time has passed following the start of the proton beam. This approach allows us to study the remaining neutrons and use simulations to derive the characteristics of the initial neutrons. The device's detection system consists of six modules containing 88 scintillator modules each, for a total of 528 individual scintillators. To prevent the introduction of electromagnetic noise, the Aberdeen Tunnel laboratory is equipped with a metal mesh ceiling. To compensate for the target's thickness, our data is corrected through calibration, taking into account the difference between the measured data and simulations of free-flight neutrons. The data collected so far demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing a notable alignment with previous research on free-flight neutrons.

Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey, which aims to pair the capabilities of the TESS and Keck/NIRSpec to achieve this goal. By combining their strengths, we can obtain a comprehensive understanding of the properties and behavior of exoplanets. In this research, we outline our target selection criteria and present the characteristics of the exoplanets we have chosen for further study. These targets, which comprise 103 planets or asteroid candidates around 86 stars, were identified through their brightness and proximity to Earth. We selected stars with a high likelihood of hosting planets in small to medium-sized stellar systems and excluded those with prominent proper motion or contamination from nearby stars. Furthermore, we selected targets with a high potential for contributing to the advancement of scientific knowledge in various fields of astrophysics and planet formation and evolution.

The growth of Information Technology across all sectors brings significant benefits, but it also introduces security threats that necessitate innovative solutions. One critical aspect of enterprise security involves identifying and verifying the information listed on identification documents, but this can be a laborious process due to the large volume of data involved. To streamline this process and enhance identification document analysis efficiency, this research introduces an extraction tool aimed at ID card data, utilizing a combination of Optical Character Recognition and Natural Language Processing to facilitate easier verification and data use. This technology is specifically designed for extracting data from Indonesian ID cards, but it has equal potential applicability to other identification documents across various countries.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state using path integral methods with a focus on driving forces. Calculations of position, energy, and expectation values of the x and y components of the spin-1/2 particle's position were consistently accurate when compared to established quantum mechanics results. Additionally, driving forces were successfully handled up to 10 times the harmonic oscillator's natural frequency. The developed framework effectively addresses limitations of classical simulations based on the classical path approximation method.

Rapid changes in the rotation velocities of small asteroids can be caused by the Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect. By combining observations from various sources, research reveals that asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro are spinning very quickly. While this may seem like a result of the YORP effect, more data is needed to confirm this conclusion due to the long timescales involved. It's also important to note that YORP can cause slower changes in an asteroid's rotation rate, leading to its eventual stabilization.

Social media has become a primary vehicle for political opinion expression and shaping public opinion in recent years. Instagram, being a visual social network with influencer marketing potential, is increasingly being used by high-profile individuals and brands to spread political messages and engage with followers in discussions. This study examines how political conversations evolve over time in Instagram comment sections under the influence of users with varying levels of social status, such as anonymous contributors, casual followers, and influential account holders. Our analysis reveals distinct discussion dynamics based on the number of participants, with shorter discussions featuring more collaborative and coherent exchanges, while longer discussions include more confrontational language and personal attacks. Notably, research has shown that online discussions similar to those analyzed here tended to shift towards supporting the initial poster's viewpoint, a phenomenon known as the "online poll effect." Conversely, our findings indicate that in the context of Instagram comment sections, the majority of discussions deviate from this expected pattern, with the majority of participants ultimately switching to opposing the initial view.

We show that any infinite collection of surface homeomorphisms, exchanging Lebesgue measurable subsets of a fixed surface through quasi-arithmetically simple paths, fails to achieve compactness within the Roelcke precompactness topology.

Determining the properties of nearby M-dwarfs is crucial for studying the smallest stars in the galaxy and those most similar to the smallest exoplanets that might orbit these stars. However, accurately assessing the stellar parameters of M-dwarfs based on M-band spectra is challenging due to the absence of clear features, unlike for A-G stars. In contrast, the analysis of ultraviolet spectra offers detailed information on a star's composition and can provide insights into a star's mass. By analyzing UV spectra, researchers can determine the properties of M-dwarfs with greater precision than other methods. This paper presents the methodology used to assess the parameters of M-dwarfs based on UV spectra, including how stellar activity affects the results and how rotation is factored into the analysis. It also presents a sample of 16 M-dwarfs with comprehensive data, along with comparisons to existing M-dwarf catalogs. The study demonstrates that the parameters derived from UV spectra are reliable, and future telescopes with higher sensitivity will significantly improve the accuracy of this assessment. The paper also outlines the rationale and methodology for selecting a sample of low-mass stars with well-determined parameters, which will be the subject of analysis in a forthcoming study on the properties of M-dwarfs.

Recent breakthroughs in nanophotonics research have led to the creation of subwavelength ripples pattern, effectively utilized for polarization-based functions such as light reflection and deflection. Initially produced through laser processing, the exact manipulation of s- and p-polarized components in this process has only been theoretically understood. A new model demonstrates a dual metasurface's capacity to control the formation of ripples by differentially directing s- and p-polarized components, enabling efficient creation of line ripples in both directions. By adjusting the carrier surface and relative angles between the two components, line ripples can be precisely controlled for both directions. This finding has the potential to expand line ripples fabrication beyond ultraviolet laser technology, enabling production on any material with a compatible carrier surface.

A key characteristic of relational data is its ability to contain self-referential tables, allowing queries that join a table to a derived version of itself. In this research, we explore the theoretical limitations of querying such tables with respect to containment relationships. By assuming a specific, well-understood containment relationship between two tables, we can determine which queries can efficiently process the contained table by comparing them to a modified version of the original query. Our focus on self-contained tables enables us to consider more complex queries involving self-referential tables. In doing so, we develop a more nuanced understanding of the challenges associated with querying self-referential databases. In particular, we show that neither the ability to efficiently process a query nor the complexity of that query is necessarily indicative of difficulty when dealing with contained data. Furthermore, we identify specific query patterns that can lead to inefficient processing even in the absence of self-referential data and highlight the limitations of current containment knowledge bases in relation to self-referential databases. In order to address these limitations, we introduce a novel approach to representing and querying self-referential databases using containment relationships. This approach is evaluated using both theoretical and practical assessments.

Fair behaviour in reactive systems can be described using fair solvability conditions for an extended Buchi automaton, a type of non-deterministic finite-state machine that accepts infinite word inputs. These conditions ensure that a specific pattern is met indefinitely, once it has been met temporarily, and can be used to resolve decision-making conflicts within reactive systems that interact with their environment. Our research focuses on combining fair solvability conditions with rational transition functions, representing the system's reactions, by selecting a specific fair method that can be executed by the system. This execution method must be computable, allowing the system to make data-driven decisions during its interactions with the environment. Satisfying fair solvability conditions using rational transition functions is an open problem, and our research aims to explore various fair conditions and their combinations to determine whether they have a fair solution that conforms to rational transition functions. We provide a novel approach to solving this problem for conditions that have already been solved, and our approach can be applied to any condition that can be solved using an algorithm that only considers even-length suffixes of the input word. Our approach combines condition solutions by considering the limits to which fair solutions can be flexibly adjusted, and it demonstrates that solving fair conditions with rational transition functions is a relatively simple problem compared to the complexity of the fair condition itself.

Using 79.7 pb of intensity front data, this study measures the amplitude of specific $B$ decay modes, namely $B^0$ to $K^{*0}$ times the conjugate, and determines the branching fraction of the $B^0$ to $K^{*0}$ times the conjugate decay mode by initially separating the $S$ and $P$ wave components of the amplitude, we find the magnitude of the $P$-wave component to be 0.0291 ± 0.0087, and the branching fraction for the $P$-wave component to be (3.67 ± 0.85) × 10^-5, and the total branching fraction to be (1.16 ± 0.20) × 10^-5, all at the 95% confidence level.

A complex system's behavior can be characterized by multiple coexisting attractors in both static and dynamic settings. Although this phenomenon may seem complex, it can be further elaborated when simplified to a bi-stable scenario. Our study specifically examines a scenario with three coexisting attractors in a dynamic system. We identify a particular configuration in a two-dimensional projection where two stable points become unstable, giving rise to a transient scenario that leads to a transient pattern. We then observe a specific setup in the three-dimensional original system. We define a particular two-dimensional projection where one stable point becomes unstable, resulting in a dual-stable scenario. We discover a particular setup in this scenario that leads to a transient pattern, giving it the name bradyphasic pattern. We find this pattern to occur when a specific point is precisely reached in the dual-stable scenario. We also find that this pattern can emerge from any point that lies on a specific line in the dual-stable scenario. We further find that the bradyphasic pattern can occur when a specific point is precisely reached in any point that lies on a specific line in the dual-stable scenario. We then observe that the bradyphasic pattern can occur when a specific point is precisely reached in any point that lies on a specific line in the dual-stable scenario, which can also occur when a specific point is precisely reached in any point that lies on a specific line in the dual-stable scenario.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation around the median, addressing a longstanding challenge in statistical research.  Developing an unbiased estimator for this quantity has been a recognized difficulty, as it does not comply with the criteria set by the influence function, unless it is based on a specific family of distributions.  A novel approach creates a bias-corrected estimator for the median absolute deviation, leveraging the properties of a specific norm, and it is shown that it achieves the optimal asymptotic distribution under normal conditions, meeting the standards of consistency, efficiency, and accuracy.  A simulation study evaluates the performance of this estimator in comparison to existing alternatives.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

Deep neural networks with sigmoid or tanh units typically rely on overwhelming numbers of parameters to model non-linear relationships, but our research shows that incorporating modulated periodic activations into the units significantly reduces the necessary parameters by approximately 50 times. When applied to a basic fully connected network for image classification, this results in a 10 times decrease in parameters. Notably, our model achieves exceptional performance on MNIST and comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with only 1.5 million parameters, an improvement of over 100 times in parameter efficiency. When fine-tuning VGG16 on CIFAR-10, our model achieves a top-performing accuracy of 82.31%. Furthermore, our model's increased generalizability enables minimal loss of accuracy when we introduce random obstacles in the training data and significantly fewer parameters to adapt to changes in composition, allowing for local functional connectivity to drive generalization.

A long-standing question in neuroscience research is the origin of the animacy perception phenomenon observed in humans, specifically within the ventral temporal cortex. Our study reveals a distinct pattern of animacy preferences along the medial-lateral axis of the lateral occipital complex (LOC). This discovery challenges existing theories that attribute animacy gradients to factors such as face detection or movement intensity. Instead, we find that a distinct animacy-sensitive area exists within the medial part of the lateral occipital complex. Further analysis of fMRI data collected during free exploration of nature video clips showed that this area is responsible for processing a wide range of animate entities beyond humans and categorical effects are present across multiple animate categories. These findings are consistent with outcomes from a separate study using eye-tracking, where subjects were asked to rate the animacy of stimuli presented at specific locations within the LOC. Collectively, our findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying animacy perception in the human brain.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a rate compatible with predictions made by the Shafere-Vented duality formula. Additionally, this outcome holds for Dirichlet L-functions.

In this research, we're expanding quantum relational Hoare logic with expectations to analyze the behavior of quantum systems that interact with dynamically changing environments. By incorporating sequential composition and weakest preconditions, we're able to solve practical quantum relational verification problems. Our approach has been demonstrated using a prototype implementation, yielding promising results in the field of quantum verification. Additionally, we're exploring potential applications of our work in verifying quantum protocols, particularly those developed by the lossy quantum protocol verifier (LQPV).

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases among populations can be significantly influenced by a few highly contagious individuals who spread the disease quickly over long distances. These super-spreader events have the potential to greatly impact epidemics by accelerating the widespread transmission of the disease. Using a mathematical framework that models a population with a small number of long-distance connectors whose movement can cover the entire population, we show that the disease's transmission speed can be substantially increased by these events, leading to even higher rates of infection in the population. Furthermore, we find that even a single super-spreader event can be enough to cause the entire population to become infected, a phenomenon we term as the'super-spreader effect'. Additionally, we observe that in populations organized in clusters, the number of super-spreaders required to infect the entire population decreases with the level of fragmentation.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with a cyclic collection of operators, labeled F, functioning across X. Our previous research demonstrated the accuracy of certain estimates concerning the cyclic collection's hypercyclic elements and their associated dimension. Building on that findings, new criteria have been established for a single operator within F to possess the same elements as the collection as a whole. Furthermore, our established criteria ensure the maximum possible dimension for the collection's common elements, providing a key insight into the composition of the collection's elements. It has also been proven that each operator within F shares the same growth rate as the collection's leading operator, providing a generalization to arbitrary closed subspaces.

The procedure for producing solar vector magnetic field data from magnetogram observations using inverse problems can be impacted by biases stemming from data characteristics and post-processing corrections in image analysis. The potential effects on magnetic field estimates should be investigated to ensure data quality meets the standards set by observational missions like PHIS. A statistical framework can be applied to assess biases in magnetic field magnitude and component estimates. However, the current approach has limitations in accounting for spatial dependencies in magnetogram observations. A case study was conducted to demonstrate the presence of biases in magnetic field component estimates and the resultant effects on vector magnetic field maps. The findings showed that conventional preprocessing steps can introduce biases in magnetic field component estimates, leading to distortions in the calculated maps. An alternative data analysis process was also tested to demonstrate the presence of biases is data-dependent. Therefore, it is essential to evaluate the impact of biases on magnetic field estimates to ensure data accuracy meets the required standards for scientific validity.

A comprehensive study has been conducted to measure radii of 146 prominent young stellar clusters in 21 nearby galaxies using high-resolution Hubble Space Telescope images from legacy programs and recent observations. The research calculates radii for each cluster, ranging from 0.17 parsecs to 34 parsecs, and constructs a local maximum of radii distribution at approximately 2 parsecs. The cluster radii depend on the parent galaxy and its characteristics, such as star formation rate and gas supply, and exhibit distinct patterns when compared to the general distribution. The study discovers a notable correlation between cluster radii and mass, as well as mass-to-light ratios, with smaller radii often found in more massive clusters. The findings also reveal varying scales of cluster formation, with smaller, more compact clusters prevalent in certain galaxies like NGC 4490, in contrast to the larger, more extended clusters found in galaxies like M51.

Using an sum-over-scales method, a novel approach to calculate the decay width of $\eta_c$ into two photons is presented. This method implies that to achieve accurate results at the scale of the heavy quark, a lattice simulation is necessary. Although this approach may seem complex, it offers a simpler way to calculate the decay width compared to existing methods. By applying an sum-over-scales method, the need to directly calculate the amplitude of the decay process is eliminated. Furthermore, the decay width can be expressed in terms of the heavy-quark mass and other physical parameters, which can be determined through lattice simulations or experimental measurements. Although the initial, coarse estimate of the decay width was already known, further refinement is necessary to ensure consistency with experimental data. This consistency is necessary to validate the approach and make the approach useful for extrapolating lattice simulations to other decay processes.

In recent years, the complex-valued neural network has proven to be a compelling alternative to the traditional real-valued neural network, offering increased model flexibility and potential improvements in model performance. This complexity extends beyond signal processing applications, where real and imaginary parts are often treated as separate inputs, to a full exploration of complex number representation. A notable benefit of using complex numbers arises during optimization, where the derivative of a complex function yields a complex value, eliminating the need to manage up and down gradients that can cause stability issues. With the exception of a few existing works, the potential of complex-valued neural networks in chemistry has yet to be explored. This work introduces a novel chemistry-oriented complex-valued neural network, designed to minimize the notorious hubbard sign issue that limits the efficient application of electronic structure theory. Our complex-valued network replaces the traditional hubbard u-parameter with a rotation matrix, facilitating efficient Taylor series expansion and differentiability without the constraints of u-sign management. Our results show that our complex-valued network achieves significant reductions in energy prediction errors, achieving an average MAE of 0.25 eV, outperforming its real-valued counterpart across multiple benchmark datasets. Our approach has been made available as an open-source code titled CUNN-chemistry, capable of handling general chemistry tasks beyond energy prediction.

Prime factorization allows the expression of any integer as a product of prime factors. Considering the sequence $a_n$ representing the number of integers within a specific range that possess a particular prime factorization, our main goal is to derive upper and lower bounds in relation to the Dickman function $\rho$. By establishing these bounds, we aim to investigate the behavior of the sequence in relation to the Dickman function $\rho$. A key observation arising from this analysis is the discovery that for sequences defined by a specific set of prime numbers, a specific relationship with the Dickman function $\rho$ holds in a range that is otherwise unaffected. A crucial finding emerging from this analysis is the demonstration that for sequences defined by all prime numbers, a specific relationship with the Dickman function $\rho$ applies only at a particular point. A further contribution of our work is the introduction of the term "fragile" to describe sequences that exhibit a specific fleeting relationship with the Dickman function $\rho$.

Given any non-erasing free monoid homomorphism $\phi$, there is a corresponding subshift complexity function $p_\phi$ derived from the original complexity function $p$. This relationship leads to the following entropy-related inequality: $h_\phi \leq h_p \leq h_\phi'$, where $h_p$, $h_\phi$, and $h_\phi'$ denote the entropy of the associated subshifts. When considering free basis changes, a similar, though less straightforward, behavior is observed. Specifically, for any non-erasing free basis change $\phi$, there is a corresponding subshift complexity function $p_\phi$ derived from the original complexity function $p$. This relationship leads to the following entropy-related inequality: $h_\phi \leq h_p \leq h_\phi'$, where $h_p$, $h_\phi$, and $h_\phi'$ denote the entropy of the associated subshifts.

To bridge the gap between training and deployment in machine learning models, it is essential to facilitate cross-task generalization without additional labeled data. A key challenge lies in adapting a model trained on labeled data from one setting to an unrelated, unlabeled test environment. This paper introduces a novel unsupervised framework for achieving cross-task generalization, leveraging a model that retrieves relevant examples from the target dataset to refine its performance on that specific task. We evaluate our method on three different test environments, demonstrating that it yields enhancements of up to 95.16% in accuracy when comparing models trained on labeled data to those trained on unrelated, unlabeled data. This includes successful applications to both image and text classification tasks.

A novel method is presented for extracting independent components from a data source with minimal human input. The proposed algorithm, m-ar-k-fast-ica, automatically determines the number of components to identify and executes this task at a critical point where performance is optimal, preventing the common issue of over-extraction seen in other methods. Furthermore, k represents a parameter that limits the number of linear transformations applied to the data, which can lead to better results when compared to applying no restrictions. The algorithm's efficiency is comparable to that of other fast ica methods, thanks to the use of a first-then approach that divides the process into two distinct stages. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

This study seeks to increase understanding of requirements engineering in the gaming sector. Despite the industry's significant economic impact, there's been a noticeable lack of research on how requirements are managed for entertainment products, including games. To address this knowledge gap, we analyzed a diverse range of games spanning platforms, genres, and regions of development. Our analysis revealed intriguing differences in development settings and the approaches used to gather requirements, including varying levels of emphasis on stakeholder collaboration, customer needs, and technical capabilities. We also examined how used design documents reflect the complexity of the software and the level of cooperation among development teams. Our findings suggest several best practices for managing requirements in the gaming sector, along with potential avenues for additional research into this area of software development.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that effectively identify optimal hyperparameters for a differentially private model in a non-private training environment is highly desirable. In this research, we introduce a new approach called Efficient Hyperparameter Optimization for Private Models (EhopPM), which systematically explores a compact set of optimal hyperparameters for the non-private model. EhopPM is particularly well-suited for large-scale experiments, as it utilizes a limited number of central processing unit (CPU) cycles and is well-financed. The results of our experiments demonstrate that the hyperparameters identified by ehopPM, our high-performance algorithm, consistently yield private models with robust accuracy levels, surpassing those achieved with an exhaustive search method. Furthermore, in comparison to alternative methods, ehopPM significantly reduces the time required for hyperparameter tuning. In addition to hyperparameter optimization, ehopPM has the potential to accelerate the development of private machine learning models by providing a reliable means of model fine-tuning.

Finite simple groups that act faithfully and transitively on the set consisting of elements from a specific subgroup within their centralizer, can be represented by a fixed Lie algebra type, namely the quantum version of $A_{n-1}$ in $A_n$ for $n \geq 2$. This discovery is made possible by analyzing the centralizer of a particular subgroup within the group in question. A key aspect of this finding involves demonstrating that the Lie algebra type $A_{n-1}$ in $A_n$ for $n \geq 2$ cannot be isomorphically mapped to $A_1$ by applying a fundamental theorem related to the Lie algebra's root system. A previously established result stating that the Lie algebra type $A_{n-1}$ in $A_n$ for $n \geq 2$ cannot be isomorphically mapped to $A_1$ by a specific type of mapping provides a crucial lie in proving this current statement. Furthermore, this information also enables proving that a specific type of structure, known as the Boolean structure, associated with the group's conjugation action, constitutes a minimal non-trivial structure of this kind.

The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly impact future weak lensing and source count analyses by providing exceptionally detailed images of the cosmos. The Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer instrument on Euclid will play a crucial role in achieving these results through the assessment of object shapes and photometric objects in four near-infrared wavebands. However, the performance of NISP will ultimately be limited by the readout noise of its detector array, especially at high signal-to-noise ratios. To mitigate this constraint, we have investigated the effect of correlated readout noise on NISP's measurements and assessed possible noise levels to ensure that NISP's measurements of celestial objects can be reliable and accurate. Based on this analysis, we have identified necessary noise reductions to minimize the impact of correlated readout noise on NISP's science data and have established a framework that can be applied to any similar astronomical instrument.

We utilized three different statistical techniques to analyze a vast dataset of more than 50,000 stars in the Milky Way's disk, focusing on their elemental composition. Each method included a cutting-edge approach using a two-component model, a proven four-component model, and a third alternative employing a robust median value for the elements in the sun. All techniques consistently produced similar results and revealed the presence of two primary populations based on their metal content. The results showed that the most metal-poor stars were concentrated in the galactic bulge region known as the "nucleos." Furthermore, the analysis revealed a distinct increase in the abundance of elements like iron, manganese, and nickel as you move towards the galactic center. The iron abundance in the galactic center was found to be higher than 0.25, which is significantly greater than the average found in the solar system. The patterns of elemental abundance varied depending on the distance from the galactic center and the altitude above the galactic plane. The most metal-rich stars with the highest iron abundance in the galactic center were found to have masses greater than two times the mass of the sun. The analysis also discovered a higher abundance of elements like aluminum and chromium in the regions near the galactic center. The results provided a detailed map of the elemental composition of the galactic disk and the galactic center, offering a clearer understanding of the formation and evolution of the galaxy.

This study examines the rapid spread of COVID-19 pandemic-related rumors on Chinese social media platforms Weibo and Douyin. To address this issue, a new social network model incorporating influence and propagation patterns is proposed. A scoring system for rumor rating was developed and tested on two datasets from 2020. Model evaluation and comparison used precision, recall, f1-score, and AIC/BIC metrics. Results showed that the proposed model outperformed existing alternatives when assessed through precision, recall, and f1-score in assessing rumor propagation patterns. Additionally, model complexity was reduced, improving performance and practical usability.

A comprehensive directory of 105 planetary nebulae (PN) was assembled using data from H-alpha maps of early-type galaxies within the Fornax cluster. This directory is based on the Halpha3D database and includes PNs surrounding the bright elliptical galaxies NGC 1399 and NGC 1404, as well as PNs in the spiral galaxy FCC 167, all of which have been previously misclassified as such. To determine the distances to these galaxies using PNs, a method was developed, first by identifying and excluding PNs associated with the galaxies by comparing their densities to those of typical galaxy PNs, and then by calculating the total number of PNs within a certain flux range. The resulting distances to NGC 1399, NGC 1404, and FCC 167 were 19.59 ± 0.30, 19.18 ± 0.30, and 19.45 ± 0.30 Mpc, respectively, all of which fell within the range of previous estimates for the Fornax cluster, and further reinforced the cluster's distance of approximately 19.5 Mpc.

Continuous flow processing operates on constantly changing data streams with no fixed end point, unlike traditional batch processing on static datasets with a defined conclusion. This work introduces LifeStream, a high-performance flow processing engine designed for periodic streams, to bridge the gap between continuous and batch processing. LifeStream leverages periodic boundaries to facilitate efficient data management, creating opportunistic platforms for running resource-intensive tasks on streaming data. We examine the advantages and challenges of flow processing and how LifeStream addresses related issues, and we report on the technical specifications and performance of our prototype. Specifically, we explore the opportunities LifeStream provides for developing applications using existing batch processing technologies, and we discuss the results of scalability and performance evaluations with large-scale datasets.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not exist under certain conditions as they require properties that are incompatible with the given conditions. The paper defines a particular type of curve called a timelike Bertrand curve and proves that such curves have specific properties, including being part of a unique curve category and having unique geometric characteristics. It also proves that a curve can only exist under a specific condition if it meets certain criteria that are theoretically impossible for a curve with certain defined characteristics. The paper demonstrates that a specific type of curve cannot exist under certain conditions as it requires properties that are incompatible with the given conditions.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications. Despite its significance, the loss function is often selected without much consideration of alternative options. A common loss function used in neural network training is the cross-entropy method, which is chosen for its mathematical convenience and proven effectiveness in multi-class classification. Although other loss functions like squared error, hinge loss, and focal loss have been proposed, they have not gained widespread acceptance. This study investigates the influence of loss function selection on classification performance. A comprehensive evaluation of seven loss functions - cross-entropy, squared error, hinge loss, focal loss, balance propotion loss, total variation loss, and soft hinge loss - has been conducted across six benchmark classification datasets. The findings show considerable variability in classification accuracy based on the loss function selected, demonstrating the importance of loss function choice. A statistical analysis reveals that the difference in performance is statistically significant, with at least one winner emerging that outperforms the cross-entropy method across all evaluated datasets.

A novel control strategy is introduced on a channel with a slanted boundary to stabilize the Navier-Stokes equations. The control mechanism, featuring a feedback loop with a rotating boundary, is designed to induce a specific rotation opposite to that of the fluid flow. When the control is applied to a particular region of the channel, centered around the midpoint, it is shown that it can suppress fluid vortex generation and instability. Furthermore, when the control is extended to the entire channel, a condition is derived that guarantees the convergence of fluid flow to a state of rest. A key aspect of this finding is that no symmetry in the boundary is required, explaining the term "slanted boundary feedback controllers".

This research aims to study the thermomechanical behavior of strain-induced crystallization in polypropylene during drawing processes. Crystallization is known to influence final product quality, thus predicting crystallization is crucial for optimizing processing conditions. However, modeling crystallization is complex due to interacting mechanical and thermal effects. The proposed model splits the process into two phases: rapid cold drawing and subsequent slow cooling. During cold drawing, crystallization is modeled using a user material integration algorithm, considering nucleation and growth rates as functions of local temperature and strain. As temperatures drop, a system of partial differential equations simulates cooling, influenced by heat transfer and crystallization. Solving these equations provides insights into temperature distributions, strain, and crystallization development. Numerical simulations validated the model's capabilities, showing reliable comparison with existing experimental data, particularly regarding temperature distributions, strain, and crystallization patterns during drawing processes.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on superconducting materials, we mathematically investigate the interplay between magnetic field and triplet pairing in a nematic superconductor. Using a self-consistent magnetic field theory, we calculate the magnetic susceptibility and find that the magnitude of the susceptibility is significantly greater than one when the magnetic field is low. This increase is caused by the field-induced change in pair symmetry, which leads to a more efficient magnetic response. Notably, this effect is more pronounced at lower temperatures. Our calculations also show that both the magnetic susceptibility and the superconducting order parameter exhibit oscillatory behavior when the magnetic field is high, aligning with an earlier found Shubnikov phase.

One significant issue with human feedback in robotics tasks is that it often contains errors resulting from misperceptions, inaccurate labeling, or inconsistent percepts. To effectively utilize such feedback in learning algorithms, a more flexible and broader class of feedback called "rectifying feedback" is introduced, covering corrections for both factual and perceived errors. Our research aims to address this challenging feedback type, and we introduce a novel learning paradigm called FOFR (Learning from Online Feedback with possible Errors and Percepts). The FOFR framework models real-world feedback scenarios more realistically, as it accounts for both data and perception-related mistakes. To tackle this complex problem, an episodic FOFR algorithm is proposed, utilizing a combination of comparison and perception-correcting techniques. The proposed method is evaluated on two distinct perception tasks using the RAIL (Rectifying and error-tolerant At-a-distance Inference Learning) dataset, compiled from data collected by two robotic platforms. The results demonstrate that the FOFR algorithm yields more robust performance and higher learning efficiency compared to traditional learning algorithms, despite handling more complex and error-prone feedback.

In conventional differential detection using continuous-phase modulation, a phase shift in the symbol is eliminated through phase locking, but this technique's maximum phase ambiguity remains $\pi$. To exceed this limitation, the differential encoding process must be known to the receiver. This study invests in finding the optimal receiver when the receiver is aware of the differential encoding method used for phase locking at the transmitter. The investigation focuses on finding the optimal receiver when the phase locking used is in the form of BPSK, resulting in an increased phase shift of $2\pi$ and occurs under specific conditions including long code lengths, high signal-to-noise ratios and certain modulation schemes. The study shows that when the used modulation scheme complies with certain criteria such as having a low bandwidth and being used for data transmission, the increased phase shift can be achieved without any performance degradation in the receiver. However, when the used modulation scheme does not comply with these criteria, a significant performance degradation occurs in the receiver, leading us to term it as an "overloaded" receiver. Moreover, it is also shown that the performance of the receiver can be improved by adding an additional detection stage, leading us to term it as a "delay-enhanced" differential detector, without the need for changing the existing transmitter equipment. The investigation also shows that the delay-enhanced differential detector can provide a significant performance improvement of up to 6 dB in the receiver, resulting in a nearly error-free performance, whereas the conventional differential detection results in a performance that

New findings from 3D simulations of core collapses suggest that a common merger candidate, a neutron star with a high mass ratio, may not yield the predicted large gamma-ray burst (GRB) energy releases. Instead, these stars generally form black holes with significant angular momenta. If this is consistent across all high-mass ratio mergers, it may indicate a distinct subclass of black-hole forming neutron star mergers. Research suggests that in some cases, these mergers can produce high-energy GRBs with afterglows observable across various wavelengths. In such instances, the combination of gravitational waves and gamma-rays could serve as a specific signature for identifying these events. Moreover, the detection of gravitational waves and neutrinos could provide a distinct method for detecting GRBs. In contrast, low-mass ratio neutron star mergers are expected to yield less energetic GRBs with afterglows, making them more readily detectable with all multi-messenger channels. The detection of such events is predicted to occur at a rate of roughly one per year with current detectors. The success of these detections relies on the continued operation of LIGO and Virgo, as well as the extension of their sensitivity into the 1-2 $M_\odot$ mass range.

A previously reported finding, relating the ratio of thermal quantum fluctuations in the electromagnetic field to the compressibility of spacetime's vacuum, is confirmed using Rindler observers in thermal sources. The calculation of the logarithmic reduction factor $x$ is determined and shown to be equal to half the ratio of the average energy of Rindler modes to their corresponding compressibilities. The value of this ratio is confirmed as $x = \frac{1}{2}\frac{kT}{\hbar c \alpha^2}$, with $\alpha$ being the Compton wavelength of Rindler particles. Additionally, the quantum capacity of thermal sources is found to increase by a factor of $4 \alpha^2$ when compared to the vacuum case.

Current deep learning methods significantly impair in handling heavy rainfalls due to their limited training data and complex nature. Standard approaches often rely on paired training data, but collecting and labeling pairs of rainy images along with clear counterparts is extremely challenging. In contrast, our novel disentangled image translation technique requires only unpaired sets of rainy images and their clear versions for training multiple paired models. By using a shared encoder and separate decoders, our model seamlessly breaks down the rain effect into two components - encoding the clear image and decoding the rain pattern. It disentangles these elements by learning a common encoder and decoding separate pairs of images. Our model's rain elimination process translates a rainy image back into a clear image, while our rain extraction process is the inverse, starting with a clear image and adding the rain pattern. We validated our approach with extensive experiments, achieving exceptional rain removal results and preserving the original rain pattern. Our model's code and data are publicly available for download at https://github.com/ghr2002/Closing-the-Loop.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and presenting agents with a visual representation of category hierarchies. Agents are trained to predict outcomes based on these visual representations, and their performance is assessed across three diverse game environments. Our results show that reinforcement learning agents excelled in complex scenarios when trained on hierarchical tasks, and even achieved significantly better outcomes compared to training methods that focus on individual comparisons alone. Moreover, we discovered that learning from smaller, more localized clusters can yield comparable performance to training on the comprehensive dataset. This breakthrough has the potential to enhance the efficiency of human-in-the-loop learning by significantly reducing the number of comparisons required.

The concept of physicalism faces an issue known as the causal closure of the physical, which can be addressed through the proposal of physicalist models that incorporate causal relationships between physical events. A related challenge is the continuum problem, stemming from the continuous nature of physical quantities such as space and time. A proposed solution, model physicalism, can be evaluated for its effectiveness in addressing both the causal closure and continuum problems. A survey of arguments for model physicalism reveals both supportive reasons, such as its ability to resolve the causal closure issue and the impracticality of infinite precision in physical measurements, as well as counterarguments, including concerns over the lack of clear guidelines for model causal relationships and potential difficulties in reconciling model predictions with empirical findings. Ultimately, model physicalism appears to provide a coherent framework for addressing both problems; however, resolving the challenges it poses may require a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between physicalism, causality, and the continuum.

We establish a novel result concerning the extreme case of a conformally invariant integral equation recently investigated by the authors in a series of articles. Specifically, we demonstrate that, given a non-negative function u, subject to certain conditions, there exists a unique conformal transformation Phi_u of the Euclidean space R^n of degree 2-n, 0 < n < 6, for which the Q-curvature Q_{Phi_u}(x)^2 = u(x) holds true. Moreover, we prove that, given a non-negative function u, subject to specific Poisson-Joukovskii type conditions, there exists a unique conformal transformation Phi_u of the Euclidean space R^n of degree 2-n, 0 < n < 6, for which the Yamabe invariant I_{Phi_u}(x) = u(x) holds true.

Previous studies assessing substance abuse risk in adolescents relied heavily on the Five Factor Model of personality, finding significant associations with conscientiousness, neuroticism, and extraversion. This current research aims to re-examine and expand upon those findings using a revised neuroticism six-factor model, as well as exploring potential links with all five personality dimensions. Correlations were analyzed between the personality traits and substance abuse risk, along with exploratory factor analysis to group the variables in a more comprehensive manner. Results from the revised neuroticism six-factor model showed increased coherence, and relationships with personality traits were generally consistent with previous studies.
