Furthermore, we discovered that, for certain conditions, the coherent superposition of atoms and molecules could be achieved through ionization, and this effect might be utilized to facilitate molecule-to-atom transformations. Conversely, we found that laser light with specific properties could also induce a transition from atoms to molecules. These findings implications for molecule-atom atom-molecule transformations are discussed.

Our proposed DNA-storage support structure, which includes a hierarchical indexing system along with update support, is the subject of this research. This support system is designed to operate in conjunction with the Get and Put functions that are part of the basic DNA storage API. Our approach to achieving this system is based on a novel, API-compatible encoding method of data using DNA strands. A key feature of this encoding method is that it produces storage configurations with highly efficient data retrieval performance. Additionally, our indexing system uses storage configurations as query targets, which provides efficient data retrieval. We have conducted performance evaluations using actual hardware and have obtained favorable results for both insertion and retrieval operations. Our storage system can achieve 5.57KB of data retrieval within 10 seconds and 35MB of data retrieval within 150 seconds.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable perfect time-reversal symmetry. This concept has been successfully applied to optical systems, where it enables the unidirectional propagation of light through specific paths. Building upon this success, researchers are now seeking to develop optical systems that can mimic the behavior of exotic states found in solid materials, specifically nodal lines - one-dimensional topological features. Nodal lines in momentum space represent a line where the minimal gap between energy bands meets, featuring isolated loops that protect topologically protected states along its perimeter. Although initially thought to be impossible in optical systems, recent breakthroughs have made it possible to create nodal lines in both two- and three-dimensional systems. This review focuses on the theoretical principles that govern topological phenomena in optical systems, as well as recent experimental implementations of nodal lines in momentum space. It also discusses the potential of optical systems to serve as reliable platforms for testing the exotic properties of topological states predicted in solid materials.

A complex brain tumor, specifically malignant gliomas, poses significant challenges in surgical treatment due to its unpredictable nature.  Reoccurrence rates as high as 50% highlight the limitations of current diagnosis methods.  Advances in deep learning have improved accuracy in tumor segmentation, but attempts to move beyond segmentation to classify tumor type and aggressiveness have been hindered by image noise and variability in tumor appearance.  Our research proposes a novel multi-task attention directed network, providing a framework for simultaneously performing tumor segmentation and classification.  To address issues with overfitting and data sparsity, our model leverages a combination of 2D and 3D convolutional layers.  The proposed attention directed direct supervision strategy helps model both tasks by eliminating the need for separate learning pathways.  The model is trained using the HGG dataset from the MICCAI BRATS challenge, and our experiments show improved performance in both segmentation and classification when compared to state-of-the-art segmentation models.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in the field of computer vision by integrating rendering techniques into maximum likelihood optimization methods. This research differentiates shadow computation in photometric stereo and reconstructs detailed surface normals from images, accounting for shadows. A novel approach was developed to model shadows by treating them as occlusions, extending the approach to surface reconstruction problems. A demonstration of the approach's effectiveness was shown on synthetic data, and it was applied to real-world data using the LS-SVM tool. The approach demonstrated improved performance, particularly on difficult-to-reconstruct areas, and was adaptable to various lighting conditions.

Broadcasted video footage, particularly from TV sources, employs an interlacing scanning method, alternating between odd and even numbered video lines in successive frames. This research aims at refining image processing techniques used for deinterlacing, specifically motion areas, through a real-time AI-powered approach, facilitating seamless integration with video restoration techniques. By leveraging deep learning, the proposed system effectively eliminates interlacing distortion in motion-filled frames, extending to video decoding that skips deinterlacing, thereby preserving video playback continuity. Real-time performance of this implementation is achieved on existing hardware platforms. Comparative evaluations against conventional methods, including those using advanced techniques, have shown the proposed system's superiority in both visual quality and processing speed.

Using the non-relativistic and relativistic mean field models, our study calculates the root mean square radius of the neutron's spatial distribution for various heavy neutron rich nuclei, and finds that the predictions from both models differ significantly, highlighting the need to distinguish between relativistic and non-relativistic models in the interpretation of experimental data from electromagnetic probes of nuclei.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for both off-line river crossing planning and real-time off-road navigation. By combining deep learning with the simplicity of linear equation solving, we develop a rapid shallow water equations solver and propose the RriverFlowVelocity predictor, which provides precise river flow velocity data for various scenarios, including linear cases, nonlinear cases with smooth surfaces, and cases with flowing water over smooth and rough ground. The RriverFlowVelocity predictor is user-friendly, easy to train, and efficient to implement, delivering exceptional performance in both prediction speed and model complexity.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to
encompass a broader range of lighting details. This technique can be achieved through
the automatic collaboration of two smartphone components: the operating system and
the camera software. Our proposed approach is a pioneering attempt to automate and
unify the process for both iOS and Android devices. Our method involves a novel
exposure selection algorithm, inspired by the principles of image entropy, as well
as a unique fusion technique. To validate our approach, we conducted an informal
user study and collected feedback from 15 participants. Our results demonstrate our
method's effectiveness and efficiency, enabling seamless HDR creation via smartphones.

Causal learning, a subfield of machine learning focused on uncovering cause-and-effect relationships, is navigating Profound Learning's emerging landscape. Profound Learning is characterized by massive, high-dimensional datasets with few distinct features, which forces our understanding of causality to adapt in several ways. This report explores the interplay between causality and machine learning in this era, highlighting the new challenges and opportunities presented by Profeld's unique dataset architecture. It also introduces a series of open research questions and proposes a novel framework for studying causality through machine learning from a Profeld perspective.

Research on temperature distributions within gas-solid fluidized beds has been the subject of numerous studies. Despite this, temperature arrangements in beds with settled particles still pose a mystery. Utilizing the capabilities of rapid magnetic resonance imaging, a novel method has been introduced to study temperature patterns. Initial experiments conducted using this technique revealed the emergence of symmetric temperature patterns when a heated surface was positioned perpendicular to a flow of cooler air. Further investigation explored the effects of increasing heat input and varied the arrangement of particles within the bed. Results indicate that highly irregular particle distributions lead to enhanced mixing, revealed through increased temperature contrasts when tested against a settled bed. Data obtained from these experiments have the potential to be useful in validating computational models used for heat transfer calculations.

This note presents a higher rank analog of the b-principle, incorporating a sensitive structure that is robust in a fragile manner. Specifically, we establish a consequence of the Madsen-Weiss theorem by demonstrating that a specific embedding that respects flatness can be achieved for a particular category of manifolds. Our proof relies on a sophisticated application of category theory to simplify a complex functor, ultimately involving intricate calculations in motivic cohomology. Additionally, we derive a consequence regarding oriented surface bundles with exceptional singularities.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of different algebraic preconditioners for modeling heart movement. Due to the complexity of heart tissue, this problem is highly nonlinear and requires significant scaling to simulate full heart cycles. This task becomes even more challenging due to the necessity of solving thousands of linear systems for each iteration. Our study utilizes a widely accepted model for heart tissue simulation and adapts it to a highly scalable computational framework. We test three different broad categories of preconditioners - block-based, incomplete factorization, and structure-exploiting - to determine which ones yield the fastest results and widest convergence range across various levels of system size and degree of parallelization. Our findings indicate that the best performance is achieved by a type of block-based preconditioner when solving systems with relatively small subdomains, while for larger subdomains, an alternative block-based method or a specific type of incomplete factorization preconditioner may perform better, albeit with narrower convergence ranges.

Research on random Young diagrams generated by independent, identically distributed entries has traditionally required that the diagram components not overlap. This study relaxes that constraint, allowing negative entries to create crossings. By leveraging a permutation-based approach, the eigenvalue fluctuations of associated Hermitian matrices are shown to follow a more complex distribution linked to the M\"obius function and non-crossing partitions. A key finding demonstrates that when the Riemann hypothesis holds, these fluctuations converge as expected to the Airy minimum and double Airy minimum modes. However, without this hypothesis, the mini-max formulation fails to yield this result. Instead, a different strategy is used to analyze the probability measure, ultimately leading to an alternative, albeit more complex proof of the convergence claim.

Persuasive marketing videos are utilized to influence consumers' choices in order to boost product sales and service usage. Creating such videos through artificial intelligence has become a significant task for businesses in competitive markets. Writing persuasive text has been the focus of numerous studies, but research on persuasive visual content is limited, and the combination of both is even less explored. This article provides an in-depth overview of AI-based persuasive video generation, discussing various approaches, including feature extraction using neural networks, sequence-to-sequence models, and transformer architecture, and highlighting the scarcity of related studies combining computer vision and natural language processing. It also outlines promising directions for future research in this area.

Users of mainstream encryption systems, such as TLS, regularly encounter uncertainty in evaluating the security of their connection. This study aims to quantify users' confidence in the security of their internet session and explore the underlying reasons for their perceptions. Through a combination of laboratory-based research and online surveys, this study reveals that users' trust in security is often based on factors other than actual security measures. These findings suggest that vendors should prioritize displaying security indicators that align with users' real-world experiences and preferences. Furthermore, the study recommends that security experts focus on addressing users' subjective concerns rather than their objective security needs.

Recently, researchers have been interested in combining acoustic and optical methods to create novel acoustic phenomena on the microscale. A novel approach uses laser-written structures in photostrictive polymers to create microscale acoustic periodic structures that interact with light in unique ways. By utilizing two-photon laser polymerization, it's possible to design intricate patterns in the form of hyperbolic metamaterials through the formation of triangular structures. Numerical modeling indicates that these structures can generate a new type of acoustic metagrating effect when exposed to ultraviolet light, where an anomalous reflection of acoustic waves occurs even when normal incidence is maintained. This phenomenon is further confirmed by a holographic setup capable of producing a high-frequency acoustic wave. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the potential for similar novel acoustic phenomena to be produced in other environments using different laser techniques.

Standard diffusion models rely heavily on the principle of detailed balance, which, in the case of Brownian motion, leads to the satisfaction of Gaussian distribution properties. However, Gaussianity is lost when spatial mobility varies randomly, a scenario studied using fractional Brownian motion with time-dependent scaling factors. Notably, superdiffusion can arise from both high-variance fluctuations and localized exploration, demonstrated through simulations and analytical approaches using scaling relations and stochastic differential equation transformations.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a complex system of interacting modes to be decomposed into independent, simpler two-mode interactions, which can be analyzed individually. By analyzing these two-mode interactions, key phenomena resulting from mode-mode interaction, such as four-wave mixing, are well explained. The developed framework provides a practical tool for researching optical communication systems based on Kerr nonlinearity.

A key role in control system stability proof is played by control Lyapunov functions (CLFs). They enable the use of a energy-based approach to demonstrate asymptotic stability and allow for the implementation of a controller that meets the requirements of the Lyapunov theorem. A natural extension of the concept of CLF is control warehouse functions (CWF), which can establish conditions for systems with high-dimensional state spaces to converge to a specific equilibrium point. A previously unexplored concept, first presented in this study, is the notion of state-independent control storage functions (ICSF), which can guarantee stability in systems where state information is absent. A primary focus of this paper is on developing CWF and ICSF theories and examining their connections to CLF and CLSF. Additionally, this study investigates how closed-loop system properties can lead to the existence of CWF, CLF, and ICSF. A novel result established in this paper demonstrates that an otherwise unbounded linear control system can achieve asymptotic state feedback using a state-dependent CLF. However, this control system can only be stabilized through an ICSF by allowing its state to become unbounded.

This research proposes a novel deep learning approach using a generative adversarial network (GAN) to significantly enhance the resolution of fluid flow images in experiments limited by resolution constraints. By leveraging large-scale numerical simulation data as training resources, our model can accurately recreate high-resolution images from low-resolution experimentally obtained images of turbulent flow at different Reynolds numbers. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields precise results even when trained and tested at distinct Reynolds numbers, showcasing the model's potential to enhance the resolution of experimentally obtained images in various scenarios.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding my previous views on the quantum theory, specifically regarding the application of Huygens' principle in deriving the wave formula. It was incorrectly assumed that the flux of the wave relative to time would be a measure of probability. However, this interpretation led to an inconsistent result, implying that the probability would decrease over time, contradicting the established stability of energy levels. Another issue arose from an oversimplified treatment of nodal points, which do not follow the predicted pattern under this interpretation. Additionally, the use of flux to determine energy levels was found to be too restrictive, unable to accommodate the variety of levels observed in more complex systems. Furthermore, the association of positive flux with stable states and negative flux with unstable states proved too absolute, given the existence of doubly degenerate states. The paper concludes by presenting a revised, more flexible equation that takes into account both the amplitude and the phase of the wave function.

In deep neural network-based classification, overconfidence in predictions is a pervasive issue, particularly in the open-world setting where novel unknown categories may emerge. This research introduces a novel concept, energy-driven uncertainty, to address this challenge. A mathematical framework is developed to ensure the energy-driven uncertainty remains contained within a specific domain, effectively isolating predictions from unknown categories. An energy-based uncertainty model is devised to facilitate efficient computation of this uncertainty. The proposed approach is integrated into a multi-task learning framework, utilizing energy-driven uncertainty to differentiate predictions from unknown categories. The approach is evaluated on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets, demonstrating its computational efficacy and versatile applicability.

In the context of rapidly changing and vast task spaces, lifelong reinforcement learning (LRL) is a critical approach that focuses on adaptive, continuous learning across an infinite array of tasks. Despite ongoing research, LRL is yet to be supported by a comprehensive, unified evaluation framework that addresses multiple challenge settings simultaneously. To bridge this gap, we introduce Lifelong Reinforcement Learning Evaluation Environment (L2Explorer), an exhaustive evaluation platform consisting of multiple integrated benchmarks that incorporate various LRL challenges, conditions, and performance metrics. L2Explorer is designed to be versatile and user-friendly, allowing developers to easily create custom LRL environments through a proprietary procedural generation method. We showcase the versatility of L2Explorer by conducting a comprehensive assessment of several cutting-edge LRL algorithms across diverse evaluation scenarios. Additionally, we provide open-source implementations of these methods and the complete evaluation environment on our repository, inviting the community to collaborate and contribute to the advancement of LRL evaluation standards.

Understanding business processes relies on process analysis, research, and case studies, but due to their complexity, other approaches such as declarative process models become more appealing for exploration and understanding purposes.  Our approach utilizes a type of declarative process model called DIVE, creates a monitoring technique using Dynamic Role-Based Access Control, and an inquiry language to enable the analysis of these processes.  We demonstrate this approach by applying it to real-world processes from previous research and finding processes.  Our approach provides solutions for process assessment tools, helping to prevent process issues and facilitate process learning through example cases.  It also facilitates process understanding by providing a more accessible representation of processes.  We examine the practical applications and challenges of this approach in an empirical study of declarative processes.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain conditions can lead to a sudden shift from localization to delocalization. Our theory and experimental results show that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, there is an unusual phenomenon where this transition becomes reversible, swapping the positions of the quasiperiodic and periodic samples, for both a quasiperiodic diamond photonic crystal and a periodic diamond structure. This means that when we switch from a quasiperiodic diamond structure to a quasiperiodic diamond with a longer lattice period, a wave with a longer wavelength will suddenly shift from being trapped to freely moving, and vice versa. Additionally, our experimental results also indicate that this transition can occur non-robustly by relying on the interplay between different frequency quasiperiodic states, allowing for a deeper understanding of this phenomenon.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. The data processing system for Liger will serve as a central hub, responsible for managing science data production, configuring the device, and supervising operations. We have designed the data processing system with a focus on flexibility, given the device's versatile nature, and have established software interfaces to integrate the system with relevant facilities at the observatory.

Optical systems based on spatial mode demultiplexing are being explored for their potential in ultra-high capacity optical communications. A key limitation of this technology is the minimum resolvable distance between modes, which is determined by the diffraction-limited system and cannot be improved through lens systems. Theoretical limitations of this principle are the focus of our study, and our findings reveal that the minimum resolvable distance can be less than the diffraction-limited value, potentially reducing the required lens size and the associated costs. Experiments using a custom-built system supported our hypothesis, and the results show that the minimum resolvable distance can be as small as half the conventional limit, achieved by collecting specific mode spacings and reducing the associated noise. The achieved super-resolution corresponds to a data transfer rate increase of 10 Gbps for a 64 GBaud 16-QAM signal. The challenge of reducing the required lens size is addressed by considering bi-photon measurements, which offer a potential solution by enabling the rejection of quantum fluctuations and recovery of lost signal, thereby enabling high-speed data transfer. The findings of our study have the potential to enhance the capacity of optical communications systems based on spatial mode demultiplexing.

This work builds on a previous finding that certain algebraic structures, specifically sheaves of nilpotent sections for a universal extension of the tangent bundle, are independent of the choice of universal extension. A similar independence of moduli space interpretations was recently established over bases with a specific characteristic. This research expands those results to bases without that specific characteristic. A key ingredient used here is a previous theorem regarding the independence of algebraic structures when using a specific type of algebraic structure, specifically sheaves of nilpotent sections for a universal extension of the tangent bundle. That theorem was previously proven for base fields with a specific characteristic. A new result expands that proof to base fields without that specific characteristic. A similar result for the moduli spaces of genus zero with marked points was also recently established over bases with a specific characteristic. This research expands those results to bases without that specific characteristic. A crucial tool used here is a previous theorem regarding the independence of algebraic structures when using a specific type of algebraic structure, specifically sheaves of nilpotent sections for a universal extension of the tangent bundle. That theorem was previously proven for base fields with a specific characteristic.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a two-timescale ecosystem consisting of a fast-growing predator population and a slow-growing prey species. Initially, the model experiences a prolonged period of transition before eventually settling into a stable oscillatory phase. Despite the prolonged transition, the system appears to return to normal population levels. However, this finding is an illusion, as small changes in initial conditions can lead to the population going into a collapse phase due to the presence of a bifurcated equilibrium point. Therefore, the model suggests that the presence of a critical slope in the predator's consumption function acts as an early warning sign for a population collapse, leading the population into a phase of decline. The model's findings also highlight the limitations of the concept of environmental carrying capacity, as it does not account for the coexistence of populations exhibiting switching behavior.

Determining how star formation relates to galaxy mass requires examining various patterns, including the tight association between mass and star formation rate. Yet, exploring this connection at high mass ranges is complicated due to the presence of active galactic nuclei, which hinders distinction between starlight and total galaxy light. By distinguishing nuclear light using AGN diagnostics, we re-examine the relationship between mass and star formation rate in galaxies hosting an AGN within mass ranges $10^{10.3}<M_{*}<10^{11.7}$. After correcting for nuclear light, our analysis reveals that nuclear light contributes significantly to the existing discrepancy between baryonic mass and starlight mass, with a median difference of $10^{10.5}$ Measured in $M_{\odot}$. By removing nuclear light effects, our results show that the slope of the mass-star formation rate relation becomes more negative by ~0.25, thus resolving the existing issue where dust correction failed to account for nuclear light and resulted in a flat slope. Moreover, we find that dust attenuation in galaxies hosting an AGN is similar to non-AGN galaxies, which has implications for estimating the mass-star formation rate relation in the local and high-redshift universe. By further removing dust effects and considering only optical starlight within half the effective radius, our analysis shows that the mass-star formation rate relation turns over at high mass ranges ($M_{*}>10^{11.3}$) due to nuclear activity rather than dust

This paper proposes a multi-task learning approach for cross-language sentiment analysis, which enables the sharing of common representation learning for classification tasks across languages. By leveraging pre-trained neural networks in multiple languages, our approach achieves high performance on the Facebook Sentiment 140 and SemEvalAffective tasks while reducing training data requirements. Notably, our model excels particularly in low-resource language classification tests.

Distributed transactions can be repaired using two techniques: self-downgrade and self-invalidations. We examine how these methods interact with two types of concurrency controls - conflict detection and conflict resolution - in order to enhance the efficiency of repairing transactions. Additionally, we investigate how varying the degree of serializability affects repair methods, concurrency controls, and system performance. Our study indicates that certain self-downgrade and self-invalidations strategies can yield better repair outcomes, reducing the need for rollback operations. We also find that certain conflict detection and resolution approaches can facilitate more efficient repairs, either with or without considering the degree of serializability. However, our analysis reveals that other methods may lead to less efficient repairs, prompting further inquiry into potential optimizations of repair strategies.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem posits that if sets A and B, with cardinality k, have a difference set of size n, then A plus B contains a subgroup of the form p^r \* Q, with cardinality greater than or equal to (3k - 4) \* p^r, where p denotes the smallest prime dividing the difference set. In this work, we relax the requirement that sets A and B have a large cardinality in relation to the size of their difference set. Specifically, given any integer n and any sets A and B with difference sets of the same cardinality, provided that n is sufficiently large in comparison to these sets, A plus B contains a subgroup of the form p^r \* Q, with cardinality greater than or equal to (3\gamma - 4) \* p^r, where \gamma is the cardinality of A and B, and the condition that the smallest prime dividing the difference set of A must divide the difference set of B.

Consider the Gaussian process $B_{t}^{H}+t\theta$, where $B^{H}$ is a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$, and $\theta$ is in $(-\infty, +\infty)$. We have found that the probability of $B_{t}^{H}+t\theta$ having a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior is $e^{-2\theta^{2}/(1-H)^{2}}$.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we develop a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on a quantum mechanical representation. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of a linear combination of two harmonic oscillators is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The resulting calculations demonstrate the existence of a quantum floor for the energy minimum, which can be modified by adjusting the parameters of the trial wavefunction. Notably, this feature emerges independently of mass or charge, thus implying that mass or charge can be utilized to lower the energy ground state. Additionally, we examine the relation between different quantum floor states and the Henon-Heiles system's classical metastable equilibrium.

This study aims to alert healthcare professionals to potentially hazardous lung conditions in COVID-19 patients being considered for intensive care unit admission, based on images analyzed through a neural network. 

Initially, we studied how lung pathology affects ICU admission in severe cases of COVID-19. 

Further, we used a dataset containing chest X-rays and labels for potential ICU admission to train and test a neural network. 

Our findings showed that lung pathology has a significant link to ICU admission in severe cases of COVID-19. 

Additionally, lung features can serve as indicators for potential ICU admission in COVID-19 patients, as demonstrated through the neural network's accuracy. 

A feature extraction technique revealed specific attributes of lung pathology linked to ICU admission. 

Prior research has shown links between lung pathology and COVID-19 severity, but has not explored the connection with ICU admission clearly. 

Therefore, our work highlights lung pathology as a crucial factor for potential ICU admission in COVID-19 patients, and suggests using lung features as indicators in clinical settings.

The universal simplicial collection has previously been established as a fundamental concept in the study of simplicial categories. Using the Dolida functor, which maps simplicial categories to the universal simplicial collection, we can determine key properties of a simplicial category. For a simplicial category with the universal simplicial collection property, being a category that preserves the Dolida functor, we have a crucial theorem stating that the universal simplicial collection is group-like. This group-like property of the universal simplicial collection plays a crucial role in our proof of the category's presheaf-like property. We have a related corollary that demonstrates a connection between the universal simplicimal collection and the geometric realization functor. Lastly, we can use our findings to prove a categorical version of the Baecklund theorem.

This paper delves into the issue of false positives in visual relationship detection. Although significant progress has been made in recent years, the detection's performance is still limited by a high rate of incorrect classifications, particularly when considering less common relationships. To address this challenge, we first conduct a comprehensive analysis to identify patterns associated with false positives and categorize them based on the confidence of accompanying object detection classes. Our proposed approach, which incorporates a relation-aware classification loss and relies on uncertain bounding box suppression, demonstrates improvements in reducing false positives and enhancing the precision of less common relationship categories in the VCR dataset. Our model's performance is compared to a strong baseline, and the results show a notable decline in false positives and an increase in accurate classifications. Notably, our technique achieves a substantial boost in precise predictions for rare relationships, resulting in a 27% decrease in false positives and a 25% increase in accurate predictions.

In this research, we resolve the challenge of training action recognition models under limited data and low-light conditions. The issue lies in accurately classifying actions based on limited and poor-quality video samples. To tackle this, we developed a novel technique called Delta Sampling, which effectively trains action recognition models using R-BERT by sampling meaningful data points. Delta Sampling succeeds in enhancing performance for action recognition in restricted data and low-light environments. Our findings demonstrate that our technique outperforms existing methods and achieves notable improvements on three benchmark datasets, resulting in enhanced action recognition precision.

Recent advancements in AI systems, surpassing human performance in multiple areas, have achieved great success by applying unique techniques such as convolutional neural networks. These systems leverage massive parallel processing capabilities offered by Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) to achieve high speed computation. However, current neural network implementations are limited by their focus on serial data access methods, which do not utilize the full potential of FPGA programming and result in underutilized system resources. To address this limitation, this research introduces a Content Addressable Concurrent (CAC) processor that enables parallel data recognition in neural networks, enabling faster and more efficient training. The CAC processor was designed and developed, with a sample application built using the vendor-independent description. Test results showed that using the CAC processor in a program similar to AlexNet led to a 1.5 times speed increase during training and a 2 times speed increase during inference. The CAC vendor-independent description was successfully translated into the language used by the manufacturer and tested on the corresponding FPGA, yielding the mentioned performance gains.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. Our study reveals that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems. One of the galaxy's, containing a highly luminous core named DUSTY-1, has undergone significant investigation. Spitzer/IRAC and ALMA observations show that DUSTY-1 has a highly irregular disk with an inner ring radius of $\rm 1.25\ kpc$ and a mass of $\rm 1.3\times 10^{10}\ M_{\odot}$. Its inner region exhibits a massive, $\rm 10^{10}\ M_{\odot}$ bulge, indicating that it underwent a major merger in its recent star formation history. Furthermore, ALMA observations of the molecular gas reservoir of DUSTY-1 allow us to infer that it underwent a significant accretion event in the past $\rm 100\ Myr$. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that DUSTY-1 experienced a major merger that caused an irregular disk formation, leading to an increased gas accretion rate and ultimately resulting in a massive bulge formation through the major merger in its recent star formation history. This finding implies that major mergers played a crucial role in bulge formation in the early universe and that lops

We re-examine the notion that allowing neutrino masses to vary by about one part in ten thousand alters the predicted ratio of neutrino to electron masses by no more than one part in ten billion.  To achieve this, we employ a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method to analyze a random sampling of approximately 250,000 models, where we enforce the universal texture zero of flavor pattern within the context of a type-I seesaw mechanism and taking into account radiative corrections to neutrino masses.  Our analysis confirms that neutrino masses as low as 0.1 eV are consistently produced, along with sufficiently small deviations between the two neutrino masses and a sufficiently large angle of approximately theta_13 ~ 0.1 in order to accommodate the observed phenomena of neutrino oscillations, consistent with experimental data from the MICE and T2K experiments.  Our findings also support the predicted ratio of the electron to the lighter of the two neutrinos masses being within the range of 1 part in 10^11 to 1 part in 10^12, thus upholding the universal texture zero of flavor prediction.

We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation that models nucleate boiling, focuses on an interior problem, and employs a specific boundary condition. Our analysis investigates the existence, local uniqueness, and periodicity of solutions within a particular function space. Notably, we leverage the Ambrosetti-Berestycki method to identify nontrivial solutions and establish a relationship between the given data and the solutions themselves. Additionally, we establish conditions under which the solutions periodicity is guaranteed.

Current deep learning methods for program generation primarily focus on sequence-to-sequence problems, which do not account for the underlying semantics of programs. To address this limitation, our work introduces a novel approach that leverages abstract syntax trees (ASTs) to enable neural networks to learn program semantics. Building upon the success of AST-based methods, we introduce a new paradigm that enables neural networks to learn program semantics from raw source code. To achieve this, our system utilizes static code analysis to automatically create a set of structured objects from source code, providing a standardized format for program representations. By utilizing this format, neural networks can learn to generate programs based on their inherent semantics. To evaluate our approach, we developed a prototype that generates neural network programs using the TensorFlow framework. Our results show that our method yields a more reliable and efficient neural network when compared to a traditional sequence-to-sequence model.

Recently discovered solar neutrino data exhibits a distinctive decay component, indicating the presence of neutrons decaying into protons, electrons, and antineutrinos in November 2004. To complement existing analytical approaches, our numerical solution to the solar neutrino problem shows that the distinctive decay component can be explained by a sudden release of very high energy neutrons from the Sun's core on November 7, 2004. Using a simple model, we find that the observed decay flux can be matched when the released neutron decay particles' energy exceeds 156 GeV. Furthermore, we observe that this event's characteristics align with those of a gamma-ray burst observed by the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope on that day, suggesting a possible connection between the two phenomena.

In the context of relativistic hydrodynamics, linearized wave modes are examined for both conformal and non-conformal fluids across various temperatures. Compared to the leading-order approximation, the next-order correction in the conformal case is identified, which depends on the specific heat capacity of the fluid and takes opposing signs for both adiabatic and isothermal conditions. Notably, the next-order correction is temperature-dependent and non-conformal, and it emerges at a much higher order in the non-conformal case. The influence of viscosity is quantified as a fraction of the wave mode's speed, measurable as 0.26 in the high-temperature limit for both conformal and non-conformal fluids. The study also reveals that the next-order correction in the conformal case can become negative, a feature that may influence the stability of hydrodynamics in heavy-ion experiments.

Anomalous behavior in continuous dynamic systems can't be addressed using conventional methods when the process is only partially known. A crucial challenge arises in quantum state monitoring, where identifying anomalies around a reference state is key to controlling and optimizing complex physical systems. We've developed an algorithm to detect and flag anomalies in a monitored quantum state by training an encoder on a dataset of quantum states using a variation of the anomaly score formula. Our approach is particularly useful for real-time anomaly detection in large-scale experiments due to its efficient update mechanism, allowing it to handle expanding datasets easily.

A pivotal issue in cryptography and law arises when the authorities demand access to encrypted information, potentially threatening users' privacy and security. To address this concern, we examine a crucial question: can a court legally compel an individual to decrypt sensitive information, even if that action alone reveals no further evidence? Through a nuanced exploration of the Santa Clara v. Kennedy case, we identify a key principle that may provide insight, although it is not directly applicable. We then propose a more relevant analogy, the "don't trust -- verify" approach, to tackle this problem. Ultimately, we conclude that yes, a court can mandate an individual to decrypt the information, but only if it can ensure the user has access to the necessary decryption capabilities in the first place.

We have developed a comprehensive tool using Python that simulates the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD). This tool can be used to conduct thorough analyses of various existing MDI-QKD proposals as well as custom variations. It offers detailed calculations for key gain, success probability, and final key rate in scenarios with or without source side channel issues. Additionally, it can handle situations involving coherent error in the channel. Furthermore, we have employed this tool to study and simulate a novel solution to the problem of reducing the required intensity of the signal from 10 units to 1 unit, which would significantly improve the efficiency of the system.

We develop a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for a broad class of optimization problems involving ordinals and fractions, specifically those defined by the following formula: given a set of variables subject to certain constraints, find an assignment that minimizes the sum of weighted ordinals and fractions, where these weights depend on the input parameters and the variables in question. Our approach relies on a previously established relationship and involves a series of transformations, including the application of a previous PTAS framework and a novel reduction technique involving a sort of fractional rounding. We demonstrate that our approach yields a PTAS by carefully analyzing the impact of these transformations on the problem at hand. Furthermore, we believe that our result has broader implications, as it showcases a way to effectively leverage recent research on discrete fractional programming.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical approach for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant force condition. The approach is particularly adaptable to scenarios where the external force has multiple components. We have derived an explicit, high-order Lagrange-Galerkin scheme that generates precise solutions when the external force is smooth. Our method also facilitates the computation of stationary solutions, enabling the exploration of mean field games scenarios.

Artificial Neural Networks, specifically deep learning models, have significantly outperformed other systems in various tasks such as image and speech recognition, natural language processing, and recommender systems. Unfortunately, despite their impressive performance, the complexity of these neural networks renders their functionality difficult for humans to comprehend. This lack of understanding can lead to unreliable predictions being made, particularly in high-stakes environments, prompting significant interest in analyzing and explaining artificial neural networks. This review seeks to provide an overview of recent research aimed at visualizing and interpreting deep learning models, highlighting both the techniques developed and the challenges encountered. This review also explores the different methods employed to visualize artificial neural networks, including feature importance, visualization of model architecture, and post-hoc techniques. Furthermore, it discusses the various applications, constraints, and potential pathways for future research in this domain.

A recently discovered 0.5 days rotational period in the M dwarf star HU Aquari suggests that it has experienced a significant rotation speedup. Analyzing HU Aquari's light curve and a similar star named CD-42 10911, we found that it is unlikely for these stars to have achieved such fast planetary systems as a result of angular momentum transfer through a convective envelope. Instead, we found that a convective envelope depth of less than 0.8 in these stars may explain their rapid rotation. Notably, none of the fully convective stars in the Colorado-University dwarf angular momentum survey showed such fast rotation rates. This discovery has implications for the long-standing theory that stars with convective envelopes can transfer angular momentum efficiently.

The rapid dissemination of news on social media platforms overwhelms their ability to monitor and remove false news in a timely manner. Our proposed system employs a Meta Neural Process Networks architecture, combining the benefits of both neural network and graph neural network methods, allowing for the identification of new patterns in data from news titles and posting user behavior. By using a constant number of training examples from any given class and incorporating additional information about user posting history, our system's performance surpasses existing approaches. Furthermore, our model's ability to detect false news from previously unseen data sets, without requiring retraining, demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting false news from new users and posting history.

This paper examines a previously studied equation for cyclic transport that was considered in the work of Biegelke and Kuttler. We analyze and determine the development of singularities for this equation.

This paper examines a discrete time status refreshing system where the sender updates the receiver with new information at each time slot, with the time difference between two consecutive updates being a random variable. We focus on a queueing system where new information arrives according to an independent and stationary process, with service times and interarrival times following general brittle distributions. Due to the complexity of analyzing the age of information in this context, we investigate two related metrics: the newness of information and the age of information when the queue is empty. By deriving the moment generating function of these metrics, we develop an approach using convex optimization that enables us to numerically evaluate their expected values for specific distribution cases, including erlang and geometric distributions. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of varying system parameters on the performance of the system.

Recently, a new approach was developed for finding 1-tilting Yang-Baxter operators by establishing a direct connection between these operators and specific quadratic algebras possessing a set-theoretic type solution to the Yang-Baxter equation. Building upon this framework, our research identifies a broader class of quasi-bialgebras directly derived from a specific combination of such solutions. Furthermore, it has been proven that these quasi-bialgebras automatically yield 1-tilting Yang-Baxter operators. Both theoretical developments and explicit examples are covered in this study.

Recently, research on Golay complementary arrays has been expanded to
consider multiple orthogonal complementary matrices. This work builds upon
a 2019 concept by Huang et al., which introduced an 8-element Golay
complementary array using a pair of complementary matrices. Their design
used a ring structure but this work removes that constraint. We present a
new 8-element Golay complementary array design without the ring structure
and also provide a method for creating Golay complementary arrays in N-S
polarizations. Additionally, an 18-element Golay complementary array
design is presented. These designs can generate polyphase Golay complementary
arrays, providing maximum possible orthogonal complementary matrices.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process influenced by the interference of valence bonds in molecules. This interference is particularly evident in aromatic molecules due to their symmetrical structure. Research has shown that certain benzene derivatives exhibit an unusual mix of their ground states, making them suitable for displaying valley interference. A team of scientists has successfully observed valley interference in a simplified context using a silicon nanowire, although they faced challenges due to the MW gap. To overcome this obstacle, they designed a setup with a silicon core surrounded by carbon alloy interfaces. By adjusting the energy levels, they were able to swap the spins of individual atoms. This achievement has implications for developing efficient silicon-based quantum computing systems.

Complex systems composed of multiple components often follow non-linear, interdependent dynamics that affect their overall behavior. Due to the temporal dependencies and extensive range of interactions within these systems, typical linear methods fail to capture their dynamics and underlying structure. In recent years, graph neural networks have become particularly effective in analyzing complex networks, successfully uncovering hidden patterns in multiple domains. Our novel approach leverages the strength of graph neural networks to simultaneously reveal the temporal dynamics, initial conditions, and critical parameters influencing a complex system. We successfully apply this methodology to a self-created example and a well-known experimental dataset from physics, successfully identifying key variables driving the systems' behavior and capturing the underlying temporal structure. Moreover, our method facilitates predictive modeling by modeling the systems' dynamics and identifying observable early signs that can trigger its application to unrelated complex systems.

We introduce an infinite family of polynomials related to counting the number of partitions in a homotopy theoretic context. Our approach is demonstrated for specific applications concerning combinatorial objects, such as combinatorial sequences like $m(n)$ or Fubini numbers, binary trees, and grid patterns. Additionally, we explore a generalized version of these polynomials, establishing an intriguing connection to a type of homotopy theoretic construction known as the suspension functor.

Our research focuses on creating realistic simulated brain injuries for multiple trauma scenarios using a progressive adversarial variational auto-encoder. This project aims to accelerate and reduce the high costs associated with conventional physical brain injury testing, as well as facilitate efficient development and testing of advanced safety systems using artificial intelligence. By combining advanced encoding and decoding techniques with input constraints, we enhance the quality of our simulations and ensure accurate replication of complex brain-injury scenarios. Our model consists of two modules: the encoder, which converts brain-scan data into injury severity classifications, and the decoder, which generates simulated scan data based on those classifications. Through training with limited and varied scanned data, our model successfully produces highly realistic simulated scans that accurately replicate actual brain scans corresponding to specific injury severities as verified by expert neurosurgeons and radiologists. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model's simulated brain scans accurately replicate physical brain-injury symptoms associated with specific injury paths and locations, and integrate it into a full system simulation that accurately predicts actual brain scans and associated physical symptoms.

A specific type of entanglement, unextendible product states, has unique properties that make its investigation worthwhile. Our research introduces three novel, robust forms of quantum nonlocality that are closely related to unextendible product bases, and we demonstrate examples of these nonlocality phenomena in 2x2x2 tripartite systems. Furthermore, we prove that these forms of quantum nonlocality have significant implications for the creation of unextendible product bases, and we provide a framework for identifying robust quantum nonlocality in systems of any size.

The rapid development and availability of affordable astrobots open up possibilities for widespread deployment in future sky surveys like the SDSS-V. To ensure the effectiveness of these surveys, it will be crucial to maintain the consistency of measurements across all telescopes involved. This requirement necessitates the implementation of coordinated movements among the astrobots in each net. To achieve this, we have developed a method based on rigorous mathematical principles to guarantee that the coordinated actions of the astrobots do not compromise the precision of measurements. Utilizing actual data from the SDSS-V astrobot configurations, we have theoretically and experimentally validated the safety and reliability of our method in ensuring that the measurements remain consistent across all telescopes. The safety proof ensures that all possible measurement errors always fall within predetermined limits of accuracy, while the experimental validation involves conducting repeated astrobot movements and accurately comparing the measurements obtained with those from a lead telescope. The success of our approach has significant implications, as it enables the creation of coordinated movement paths that do not pose any risk of compromising the measurement precision, a capability that will be essential for the SDSS-V.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, the native GP 2 language lacks type safety, leading to the creation of the GP 2 Compiler to ensure secure code execution. Despite its effectiveness, the compiler introduces performance bottlenecks limiting the use of computed values in loop variables and array indices. Building upon this foundation, the Enhanced GP 2 Compiler addresses this issue, enabling more expansive code execution while maintaining ease of use and overall compiler benefits.

Self-supervised learning allows models to be trained without labeled data, using contrastive learning to learn from naturally occurring contrasts in the data. In this work, we analyze popular contrastive learning methods like momentum contrast, relational contrast, and expository contrast, revealing their equivalence to a single general technique that combines a contrastive loss function with a feature extractor optimization method. We demonstrate that each of these methods essentially employs the same approach but with varying momentun coefficient schedules, thereby achieving similar performance improvements. Our research enables the development of new training algorithms that strike a balance between the different methods, leading to enhanced performance. For instance, we present an unsymmetric schedule that synchronizes the feature extractor and momentun update schedules, resulting in state-of-the-art results on cifar-10s and stl-10s datasets without external data.

We establish a limitless sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into a single orbit, and this orbit consists entirely of wedges within a specific type of twisted wreath structure. Moreover, within this infinite family of graphs, we identify a distinct subgroup whose pointwise stability guarantees the existence of a locally arc-transitive action on that specific type of twisted wreath structure. Furthermore, among finite graphs sharing a particular twisted wreath structure within a specific class, we prove that only a particular graph exhibits a locally arc-transitive action, and this particular graph can be constructed using a specific subgroup within a particular twisted wreath structure within a specific class.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling is becoming increasingly prominent due to the growing availability of numerical data that includes categorical variables. In high-dimensional scenarios, the Group Lasso method is particularly effective, as it groups together irrelevant features from different categories, reducing computational burden. However, the standard Group Lasso approach often falls short when dealing with data that has highly correlated observations, such as survey respondents, web users, or biological samples, as it can lead to over-penalization and inaccurate estimation. Overcoming this challenge requires an enhanced Group Lasso framework that accounts for the inherent correlations within data sets. By modifying the Group Lasso cost function and using a more efficient convex optimization method, our framework successfully addresses this issue. Moreover, our theoretical analysis provides performance guarantees under specific conditions, and our experimental results across various synthetic and real-world data sets demonstrate the benefits of our approach. Notably, our framework yields superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, achieving more accurate model selection and estimation in multiple scenarios.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential risk of injecting harmful knowledge into these models from vast amounts of unverified text has become a significant concern. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel approach called SKILL, which enables the incorporation of structured knowledge into LLMs while preventing the injection of unbounded unstructured knowledge. By leveraging a knowledge graph and a set of pre-existing, formally defined concepts, SKILL significantly reduces the risk of introducing unwanted knowledge and allows for the incorporation of new instance-based knowledge easily. In our experiments, we show that LLMs equipped with SKILL successfully integrate new knowledge and achieve superior performance compared to standard LLMs on various tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate that SKILL models exhibit better performance on Micro-Task Learning, a more challenging and less-studied setting. Overall, our proposed approach provides a safer and more efficient way to enhance LLMs, paving the way for their applications in critical domains such as healthcare, finance, and education.

This article establishes a unified framework for nonlocal diffusion models, ensuring consistency with both local and fractional limits. By integrating fractional space-time integrals, we construct a broad family of fractional analogs. Specifically, we demonstrate that our approach yields conventional PDEs in the local case and fractional in time, fractional in space PDEs in the fractional case. To investigate these models' long-term behavior, we develop a novel approach to the Cattabriga-Samboni technique for fractional in time, fractional in space PDEs. This approach facilitates existence and uniqueness proof for our proposed framework.

When capturing a panoramic scene using a mobile device, users often take a series of horizontal shots with their device tilted to compensate for the camera's field of view. This research focuses on stitching these images together, considering the impact of gravity on parallax. Unlike existing methods that rely on expensive optimization techniques, our work presents efficient solutions for a reduced problem set, ensuring that the resulting image is both seamless and accurate. Specifically, we've developed a localized approach to calculating depth, a method to align adjacent images without the need for global configuration, and a way to combine images using approximate segmentation. This research resulted in a visible improvement to the quality of panoramic images when tested with both synthetic and real-world data.

We will investigate specific relationships between combinatorial objects - namely, partitions of integers and arrangements of points on a line - and the elimination of poles for certain Eisenstein series under the action of the Kato-Leopoldy transfer map, which relates convolution operators to zeta integrals. Our findings will enable us to derive conditions for generating nontrivial zeta functions via the transfer map.

This study develops a biophysical brain model for Parkinson's disease using marmoset monkey brain anatomy and physiology. The model is an advancement of our previous work, integrating further detailed anatomical and functional data about the marmoset monkey brain. Specifically, we incorporated finer striatal neuron connections and a more comprehensive understanding of the dopamine system. Building on existing research, we simulated key aspects of Parkinson's disease pathology, including the disruption of dopamine supply, the death of dopamine-producing neurons in the ventral tegmental area, and the subsequent abnormal functioning of the brain regions affected. Our model predicts that these pathological changes will lead to abnormal beta wave oscillations characteristic of Parkinson's disease. We validated our model by conducting computational experiments that mimic clinical interventions used to study Parkinson's disease in marmoset monkeys, including the delivery of dopamine infusions directly into the brain. Our analysis shows that our model accurately replicates the observed effects of this treatment on brain activity. Overall, our research demonstrates the potential for data-driven brain modeling to gain insights into Parkinson's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders affecting the basal ganglia.

The proliferation of mobile devices and ever-expanding internet access has surged the demand for high-performance, interactive vector map rendering. Typical map rendering techniques employ spatial anti-aliasing to minimize artifacts, ensuring a more aesthetically pleasing visual experience. However, the computation-intensive nature of this process significantly hampers performance. In our research, we mitigate this challenge by segmenting line joins into pixel-aligned triangles and incorporating sample points to achieve a more refined anti-aliasing effect, thereby preserving the aesthetic standards of high-quality rendering.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of nine ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. Initially published in 2019, the GOALS study with the Infrared Satellite Observatory (IRSI) was designed to examine the molecular gas properties of 50 z < 0.04 infrared bright galaxies, including 39 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies. Our optical IFU data with a 5.5 pixel^2 field of approximately 2.6 kpc, allowed us to investigate the two-dimensional distribution of ionized gas in our target galaxies. Preliminary results indicate that all the galaxies exhibit some level of ionized gas extension beyond their stellar disk, with two of the galaxies (Arp 192 and IC 5133) displaying prominent ionized gas arms. Our findings from the spectral analysis revealed widespread presence of the [NeIII] line, with an average ratio to H-alpha of around 0.44, whereas the [SII] line ratio varied substantially, ranging from 0.26 to 0.37. Our data also indicate significant star formation activity across the targeted areas, as deduced from the H-alpha equivalent width, which ranged from 300 to 7000 A.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. The development allows for the interpolation of scalar-valued and vector-valued functions in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and has applications in shape-preserving interpolation, data fitting using positive or convex functions, and piecewise interpolation of monotone functions.

This study introduces a novel dataset called WeatherCateg, consisting of 50,000 images that represent 10 distinct weather categories. As notable challenges in image classification - such as fog, heavy rain, snow, and hail - lack clear boundaries and frequently overlap with other conditions, collecting accurate annotations proved difficult. To ensure data quality, we employed a bespoke data augmentation technique called'semantically consistent rotation', tested the efficacy of various Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) on previously unused datasets like WeatherCateg, and conducted an in-depth examination of model performance across different weather conditions, finding that certain characteristics, such as fog's difficulty to detect and the limited presence of snow in the data, significantly impact classification results. To facilitate further research on WeatherCateg, we are making the dataset and training code accessible online.

Recently, RNN-based audio enhancement models have achieved significant success in removing background noise from single-channel audio. This success can be attributed to their ability to effectively manage noise by utilizing historical context and a long short-term memory mechanism. However, current RNN-based models face challenges due to their limited parallel processing capability and tendency to get stuck in local minima. To address these limitations, we propose a novel dual-path convolution recurrent network that combines the benefits of RNN and LSTM models. In this dual-path configuration, recurrent and convolutional components process audio segments with shorter and longer durations, respectively. Our model leverages the strengths of both types of processing and integrates their outputs using a dual-path structure. Experimental results show that our proposed model achieves superior performance to state-of-the-art RNN-based and deep learning models, surpassing them in terms of PESQ and SDR metrics in various noise scenarios.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to assess the interaction between $f(R)$ gravity and sterile neutrinos. By comparing the predictions of the $\Lambda$CDM model to the modified theories, we collect conformal coupling constant data under three neutrino mass hypotheses: zero, light, and heavy masses. The results show that the ability to distinguish between these models depends on the specific parameters and the number of degrees of freedom. When different models are compared, the ability to discriminate falls short of the threshold required by future surveys with high accuracy. However, when modeling is accurate, even a small number of systems ($N=10$) is sufficient to differentiate between models. Additionally, we found that the power spectrum multi-dimensional marginalization has little impact on the turn-around radii. Furthermore, we discovered that future surveys will be able to differentiate between models at a $5\sigma$ confidence level in a relatively short period of time.

This study introduces a two-fluid approach to modeling atmospheric convection within a single-column simulation for convectionously mixed air masses, such as occur over tropical oceans. The approach distinguishes between warm, moist air and cooler, drier air, with the goal of preventing the spurious slip of the fluid boundary. We use a high-resolution simulation of a laboratory Rayleigh-Benard cell to validate our method, as similar patterns of convection occur in both scenarios. Slightly modifying the widely adopted multi-component modelling technique to account for boundary interactions, we implemented our two-fluid approach using the MESONET model. Our simulation results demonstrate that employing this method in a practical scenario is feasible and yields a notable reduction in boundary friction at the air mass interface. Furthermore, we observed enhanced thermal diffusion and cat-eye structure formation in our simulation.

We propose a novel method for genuinely entangling two isolated particles using single-sided access to their respective Jaynes-Cummings systems. By leveraging the unique characteristics of phase cavities, we demonstrate that a genuine tripartite entanglement can be created between an uncorrelated atom and two coupled Jaynes-Cummings systems. This entanglement formation mechanism does not rely on conditional unitary operations or the exchange of classical messages between the parties involved. Furthermore, we examine the effects of various perturbations, including spontaneous emission and cavity decay, on our proposed scheme. Our analysis indicates that our approach can lead to a highly stable and robust form of tripartite entanglement.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the experiments that make up the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) research at CERN. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for determining the trajectory of particles. Although it has operated effectively throughout Run 2, some issues with the readout system required a partial restart during low-intensity collisions in 2018. To facilitate this process, a limited number of reconstructed areas were enabled for data processing. This study focuses on the reconstruction of the pilot blades within the CMS silicon pixel detector. It includes a detailed analysis of data processing systems, software, and techniques used during this process. Furthermore, it provides statistical summaries relevant to future similar protocols.

A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which is subsequently applied to the SU(2) gluon scalar sector. Following a Wick rotation to the Euclidean space, the density is calculated on the lattice and then transformed back to Minkowski space for the physical correlation function. Initial findings for a range of masses and widths within the spectral density have been determined and correspond well with previous lattice QCD analyses of the SU(2) scalar glueball.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. Using
this combined data, we tested and proposed an LSTM-based approach for sentiment classification
on a single class. Our findings demonstrate that this approach yields superior outcomes
when compared to commonly used classification techniques and the existing dataset's classification
performance. However, combining all the data led to overfitting. Therefore, we recommend
classifying sentiment on a dataset specific to research questions.

A nonlinear charged black hole exists within a non-linear context, influenced by an electric field that it generates. This study focuses on an external, linear'shade' that affects the black hole's temperature and entropy. Within the Anti-de Sitter space, the Kleine-Neumann-Zermelo law applies, maintaining heat balance by preventing heat from escaping the black hole's shade region. As a result, the temperature differential is minimized, leading to the maintenance of heat equilibrium. The entropy of the nonlinear charged black hole has been calculated under the influence of an electric field, taking the shape of a prolate ellipsoid. Additionally, calculations have been performed for a specific scenario where the electric field's impact is minimal.

In quantum systems with multiple degrees of freedom, the von Neumann entropy is often utilized to analyze entanglement. However, this approach is not sufficient on its own to provide a comprehensive understanding, as it is necessary to consider additional characteristics like the Fisher information to grasp the complexity of these systems fully. To facilitate the study of quantum states, we propose the use of a comprehensive entropy characterizing both entanglement and the asymmetry of Wigner function spectra. Initially, we investigate tomograms associated with two systems: a qutrit and a system of two qubits. By examining these tomograms, we can observe the onset of synchronization in separate cases. For the qutrit, we analyze its Wigner function and information-theoretic measures in both individual and coupled scenarios with two identical systems. Furthermore, calculations are performed to evaluate the evolution of entropy and information-theoretic quantities in the two-qubit system under consideration.

Building conversational interfaces for specific purposes requires a complex interplay between natural language understanding and deliberate, purposeful speech. Current research has made significant strides in developing open-domain dialogue systems, but little work has been done on a more advanced level of engagement, which involves responding to user roles in a more sophisticated manner. In this paper, we propose an innovative approach to enhancing open-domain dialogue systems with role specifications, which enables them to engage users in a more effective manner. To achieve this, we established a novel dataset that incorporates role specifications and utilizes a set of pre-trained language models through a loop process, which involves role-aware prompt generation, relevance filtering, and ranking of possible responses based on their relevance to the conversation and the assigned role. Our proposed system successfully demonstrated its capacity to handle role specifications in a more refined manner when compared to a baseline model, which was further validated through a user study. Furthermore, our work has implications for further enhancing the usability of conversational AI in various settings.

Effective pest management strategies are crucial for maintaining a healthy environment, minimizing chemical usage, and meeting regulatory requirements under the Environmental Protection Agency's Food Quality Protection Act. To assist in evaluating pest management tactics, a multi-criteria decision-making approach based on the Robust Optimisation method was developed. This approach was applied to a case study of managing powdery mildew and grey back beetles on strawberry plants using chemical controls and biological controls for the secondary pest. Computational results demonstrated that chemical control was the most efficient option but most prone to risk; in contrast, biological control exhibited resilience in the face of uncertainty. A comparison of the algorithms AlgoPy, PySP, and SPOT revealed that Biological Control performed best when using these methods for all scenarios tested. Furthermore, the duration of optimal solutions varied significantly, ranging from 0.38 seconds for the easiest problem to 155.08 seconds for the most complex one.

360-degree virtual tourism videos provide an immersive viewing experience but present challenges in creating descriptive subtitles due to constantly changing camera views and limited viewer focus on specific areas. Our research introduces a novel approach to predicting perspective based on subtitles, which enables effective subtitling for these videos. By analyzing visitor attention data and subtitling guidelines, we collect 6000 subtitling samples from 600 videos, forming our reference dataset. We utilize this data to train a perspective prediction model using bidirectional LSTM networks, which is integrated into a subtitling system for 360-degree video subtitles. Our evaluation demonstrates that our approach outperforms control models and meets subtitling standards, while results from user surveys indicate user preference for our system.

Tensor network methods have emerged as effective tools for studying the behavior of complex quantum systems. However, these techniques typically struggle with scaling in thermal quantum dynamics, due to the need for contracting large-scale networks representing equilibrium or time-evolved states.
